subtopic: Restrictive cardiomyopathy from hereditary hemochromatosis — iron deposition
vignette: A 58-year-old man is evaluated for a year of progressive fatigue and exertional dyspnea. His type 2 diabetes was diagnosed at age 46 and has been difficult to control, and for the past two years he has had chronic pain and stiffness in the knuckles of both index and middle fingers. On examination his blood pressure is 132/78 mmHg, pulse is 84/min, and his skin has a diffuse bronze discoloration that his wife says has darkened over several years. His jugular venous pressure is mildly elevated at 10 cm H2O, the point of maximal impulse is diffuse but not displaced, and he has trace ankle edema. Laboratory studies show ferritin 1,850 ng/mL, transferrin saturation 78%, AST 68 U/L, and normal creatinine. An ECG shows low voltage with a first-degree atrioventricular block. An echocardiogram shows a normal left ventricular ejection fraction of 58%, a mildly increased ventricular wall thickness with a speckled appearance of the myocardium, severe diastolic dysfunction with a restrictive filling pattern, and moderate biatrial enlargement.
leadIn: Which of the following mechanisms best explains this patient's cardiac findings?

options.a: Iron deposition within myocardial cells
options.b: Extracellular amyloid fibril deposition
options.c: Granulomatous inflammation of the myocardium
options.d: Myocyte vacuolization from anthracycline toxicity
options.e: Asymmetric septal myocyte disarray and hypertrophy

explanation: The echocardiogram defines the physiology: **normal ejection fraction with severe diastolic dysfunction, restrictive filling, and biatrial enlargement** — a **restrictive cardiomyopathy**. The multisystem clues then identify the cause: early type 2 diabetes, **arthritis of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints**, bronze skin, and transferrin saturation above 45% with markedly elevated ferritin point to **hereditary hemochromatosis**. In hemochromatosis, **iron deposits within myocytes** produce the speckled myocardium, stiff ventricles, low-voltage ECG, and conduction disease seen here; on cardiac MRI the myocardium shows characteristic low signal intensity.

distractorExplanations.b: Amyloidosis also causes restrictive physiology with a thick, stiff ventricle, but it does not explain the iron studies, diabetes, or MCP arthropathy, which are specific to hemochromatosis.
distractorExplanations.c: Cardiac sarcoidosis causes granulomatous infiltration with conduction disease and regional wall abnormalities, but it does not produce iron overload, bronze diabetes, or MCP arthritis.
distractorExplanations.d: Anthracycline toxicity causes a dilated cardiomyopathy with systolic dysfunction from radical-mediated myocyte injury, not a restrictive pattern with preserved ejection fraction, and nothing in the history suggests chemotherapy exposure.

teachingPoint: Restrictive cardiomyopathy with preserved ejection fraction plus diabetes, bronze skin, and second/third MCP arthritis is hereditary hemochromatosis — iron deposition within myocytes stiffens the ventricle, and phlebotomy can reverse the cardiomyopathy if caught early.

subtopic: Coronary anatomy and conduction system
vignette: A 68-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after the onset of crushing substernal chest pain radiating to his left arm. He is diaphoretic and nauseated. Blood pressure is 148/90 mm Hg and pulse is irregular at 44/min. ECG shows ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. Serum troponin I is pending.
leadIn: Occlusion of which vascular structure is the most likely cause of his bradyarrhythmia?

options.a: AV nodal branch of the left circumflex artery
options.b: First septal perforating branch of the left anterior descending artery
options.c: Posterior descending branch of the left circumflex artery
options.d: Sinus node branch of the left circumflex artery
options.e: AV nodal branch of the right coronary artery

explanation: ST elevation in leads **II, III, and aVF** localizes the infarct to the **inferior wall**, supplied by the **right coronary artery** in the large majority of patients. The RCA also gives off the branch that supplies the **AV node**, so inferior infarcts commonly produce AV nodal conduction abnormalities such as Mobitz I block, which explains his irregular bradycardia.

distractorExplanations.b: Septal perforators of the LAD supply the anteroseptal wall and bundle branches; occlusion there produces anterior ST elevation, not inferior changes.
distractorExplanations.c: The posterior descending artery arises from the RCA in most patients, but it supplies the posterior wall and does not perfuse the AV node.

teachingPoint: Inferior STEMI (II, III, aVF) = RCA occlusion; the RCA supplies the SA node in 60% and the AV node in 80-90% of patients, so bradyarrhythmias and AV block are common.

subtopic: Urea cycle — carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I deficiency
vignette: A 2-day-old girl is evaluated in the neonatal intensive care unit for hypothermia, poor feeding, and progressive obtundation. She was born at term, and the pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated. She fed well on the first day of life but became lethargic and stopped latching yesterday. On examination she is hypotonic, minimally responsive, and has a normal fontanelle without dysmorphic features. Laboratory studies show a plasma ammonia of 610 μmol/L with normal glucose, normal lactate, no anion-gap acidosis, and no ketones. Urine organic acid screening detects no orotic acid. Quantitative plasma amino acids show a citrulline concentration below the detectable limit.
leadIn: Which enzyme is most likely deficient in this infant?

options.a: Ornithine transcarbamylase
options.b: Arginase
options.c: Argininosuccinate synthetase
options.d: Argininosuccinate lyase
options.e: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I

explanation: The first step of the **urea cycle** is the mitochondrial condensation of ammonia and bicarbonate into carbamoyl phosphate, catalyzed by **carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I**, which requires **N-acetylglutamate** as an obligate allosteric activator. When CPS1 is deficient, carbamoyl phosphate is never made, so no orotic acid appears in the urine — the opposite of ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, where carbamoyl phosphate accumulates and spills into pyrimidine synthesis. The undetectable citrulline is consistent: without carbamoyl phosphate, citrulline cannot be formed, distinguishing this from the citrullinemias, in which citrulline is markedly elevated.

distractorExplanations.b: Arginase deficiency presents later in childhood with spastic diplegia and elevated arginine, not with undetectable citrulline and neonatal coma.
distractorExplanations.c: Argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency causes citrulline to accumulate to very high levels rather than disappear, so the undetectable citrulline excludes it.
distractorExplanations.d: Argininosuccinate lyase deficiency produces elevated citrulline and urinary argininosuccinic acid, neither of which is present in this infant.

teachingPoint: In neonatal hyperammonemia, orotic aciduria separates OTC deficiency (present) from CPS1 deficiency (absent); a citrulline level then separates CPS1 deficiency (undetectable) from the citrullinemias (markedly elevated).

subtopic: Visual field defects and optic pathway localization
vignette: A 44-year-old woman reports gradually bumping into doorframes on both sides over the past year. On confrontation visual field testing, she cannot identify fingers presented in the temporal fields of either eye while central and nasal fields are preserved in both eyes. Visual acuity is 20/20 in each eye, and fundoscopic examination shows bilateral optic discs with sharp margins. An MRI of the head is ordered.
leadIn: Which of the following neural elements is most likely impaired in this patient?

options.a: Left optic nerve fibers carrying ipsilateral temporal field information
options.b: Crossed fibers from the nasal hemiretinae at the optic chiasm
options.c: Left occipital cortex representing the right visual field
options.d: Decussating nasal retinal fibers at the optic chiasm
options.e: Lateral geniculate neurons of the right thalamus

explanation: **Bitemporal hemianopia** localizes to the **optic chiasm**, where the **nasal retinal fibers decussate**. Because the nasal retina receives light from the temporal visual field, loss of these crossing fibers — classically from a **pituitary adenoma** compressing the chiasm from below — knocks out the temporal field of each eye while sparing the uncrossed temporal retinal fibers. Visual acuity and disc appearance remain normal early because the macular fibers are affected only late.

distractorExplanations.a: An optic nerve lesion causes ipsilateral monocular blindness, not a bilateral field loss.
distractorExplanations.b: An optic tract lesion causes a contralateral homonymous hemianopia, a loss of the same half-field in both eyes.
distractorExplanations.c: An occipital cortex lesion produces a contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing, not bitemporal loss.
distractorExplanations.e: Lateral geniculate lesions also produce homonymous field defects reflecting the retinotopic map, not bitemporal loss.

teachingPoint: Bitemporal hemianopia = chiasmal compression (pituitary adenoma) of crossing nasal retinal fibers, which carry temporal field vision. Optic nerve = monocular blindness; optic tract/occipital = homonymous hemianopia.

subtopic: Endometriosis management after failure of first-line medical therapy
vignette: A 29-year-old nulligravid woman with endometriosis confirmed by laparoscopic biopsy 2 years ago returns for follow-up. She stopped the oral contraceptive 2 months ago because of inadequate relief. She hopes to become pregnant within the next 2 years. She is afebrile, blood pressure is 110/68 mm Hg, and pulse is 74/min. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 3-cm complex ovarian mass with diffuse low-level internal echoes and no significant flow on Doppler, consistent with an endometrioma. options.b: Begin a combined oral contraceptive with a different progestin component
options.c: Refer for laparoscopic excision of implants and the ovarian cyst

subtopic: Obstructive PFT pattern with bronchodilator reversibility
vignette: A 28-year-old man presents with a two-year history of episodic wheeze and chest tightness, most often triggered by his cat and by exercise. He has never smoked and works as a software developer. On examination he has scattered expiratory wheezes. Spirometry is performed: FEV1 is 62% of predicted, FVC is 88% of predicted, and the FEV1/FVC ratio is 0.68. Fifteen minutes after four puffs of albuterol, FEV1 increases to 79% of predicted. His chest radiograph is unremarkable.
leadIn: Which set of findings best characterizes this patient's baseline pulmonary physiology?

options.a: Obstructive pattern with increased total lung capacity and reduced DLCO
options.b: Restrictive pattern with reduced total lung capacity and reduced DLCO
options.c: Obstructive pattern with increased total lung capacity and normal DLCO
options.d: Restrictive pattern with reduced total lung capacity and normal DLCO
options.e: Obstructive pattern with elevated total lung capacity and preserved DLCO

explanation: The low **FEV1/FVC ratio** with a preserved FVC defines an **obstructive pattern**. In asthma, air trapping during exacerbations and chronic hyperinflation raise the **total lung capacity**, while the alveolar-capillary membrane remains intact, so the **DLCO is normal or even increased**. The 17% absolute improvement in FEV1 after albuterol confirms the reversibility that distinguishes asthma from most other obstructive diseases.

distractorExplanations.a: A reduced DLCO with obstruction and hyperinflation suggests emphysema, where alveolar destruction impairs gas transfer; this patient's young age, no smoking history, and reversibility point away from emphysema.
distractorExplanations.b: A restrictive pattern with reduced DLCO characterizes interstitial lung disease, where both lung volumes and gas transfer fall together; his FVC was preserved and the ratio was reduced.
distractorExplanations.d: A restrictive pattern with normal DLCO suggests chest wall disease or neuromuscular weakness, which would not produce wheezing or a post-bronchodilator response.
distractorExplanations.e: His baseline FEV1 was only 62% of predicted with a reduced ratio, so baseline spirometry is clearly abnormal.

teachingPoint: Asthma shows an obstructive pattern (low FEV1/FVC) with hyperinflation (increased TLC) and a normal or increased DLCO, plus reversibility after a bronchodilator.

subtopic: Adult coarctation of the aorta
vignette: A 27-year-old man is evaluated at a routine insurance physical after a blood pressure reading of 158/96 mm Hg in the right arm. He reports occasional exertional leg fatigue but no chest pain or dyspnea. He takes no medications and has no allergies. His father had coronary disease at age 60. Blood pressure is 156/94 mm Hg in the right arm and 148/92 mm Hg in the left arm, and 102/66 mm Hg in the legs; pulse is 70/min. Examination shows a prominent pulsation in the suprasternal notch and a soft bruit over the left interscapular area. Femoral pulses are reduced and delayed compared with the radial pulses. Transthoracic echocardiography shows a discrete narrowing of the descending thoracic aorta just distal to the left subclavian artery with a peak gradient of 45 mm Hg across the lesion, normal bicuspid valve function, and normal left ventricular systolic function.

options.a: Transcatheter stent implantation following balloon dilation of the stenotic segment
options.b: Amlodipine therapy with blood pressure reassessment in 3 months
options.c: Surgical resection with end-to-end anastomosis
options.d: Percutaneous balloon angioplasty with stent placement
options.e: Metoprolol therapy with exercise stress testing in 6 weeks

explanation: Upper-extremity hypertension with **radio-femoral delay**, a blood pressure gradient between the arms and legs, and an interscapular bruit identify **coarctation of the aorta**, confirmed by echocardiography with a gradient >20 mm Hg. distractorExplanations.b: Medical antihypertensive therapy alone is inadequate; the gradient of 45 mm Hg meets criteria for intervention.
distractorExplanations.c: Surgical repair is preferred in neonates and infants or in long-segment coarctation; in adults with a discrete lesion, stent angioplasty avoids the morbidity of thoracotomy.
distractorExplanations.e: Beta blockade does not address the obstruction, and stress testing adds nothing to an already confirmed anatomic diagnosis.

teachingPoint: Adult coarctation presents with arm-leg blood pressure discrepancy, radio-femoral delay, and interscapular bruit; a discrete native coarctation with a significant gradient is treated with percutaneous stent angioplasty.

subtopic: Thalassemia trait versus iron deficiency
vignette: A 26-year-old woman from Greece is evaluated during a pre-employment health examination. She feels well and reports no fatigue, no heavy menstrual bleeding, and a diet that includes red meat several times weekly. She takes no medications. Her physical examination is unremarkable. A complete blood count ordered as part of the examination shows hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 66 fL, red blood cell count 6.1 million/μL, and normal white blood cell and platelet counts. The peripheral smear shows microcytic cells with minimal variation in shape and no target cells. Ferritin is 85 ng/mL, serum iron is 95 μg/dL, and transferrin saturation is 30%.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

options.a: Order hemoglobin electrophoresis
options.b: Measure soluble transferrin receptor concentration
options.c: Perform upper and lower gastrointestinal endoscopy
options.d: Test for abnormal hemoglobin variants using gel electrophoresis
options.e: Repeat the complete blood count in 6 months

explanation: This patient's iron studies are normal, so her **microcytosis is not iron deficiency**. The key clue is **disproportionate microcytosis**: a mean corpuscular volume of 66 fL with a hemoglobin of 11.9 g/dL is far more microcytosis than the degree of anemia explains, and the **elevated red blood cell count** is characteristic of thalassemia trait, in which the marrow compensates for small cells by producing more of them. Her Mediterranean ancestry and the **Mentzer index** (MCV divided by RBC count, less than 13) both point to **thalassemia trait**. **Hemoglobin electrophoresis** is the confirmatory study, showing an elevated hemoglobin A2 in beta-thalassemia trait. No iron should be given, since her stores are already normal.

distractorExplanations.b: Soluble transferrin receptor is elevated in iron deficiency, which her normal iron studies already exclude.
distractorExplanations.c: Endoscopic evaluation is indicated for iron deficiency anemia in men and postmenopausal women; this premenopausal woman has no iron deficiency at all.
distractorExplanations.d: Iron therapy would do nothing here because her ferritin and iron studies are normal, and it risks iron overload in a patient who does not need it.
distractorExplanations.e: Deferring evaluation leaves a heritable hemoglobinopathy, relevant to future pregnancy counseling, undiagnosed.

teachingPoint: Microcytosis out of proportion to anemia, an elevated RBC count, normal iron studies, and a Mentzer index under 13 point to thalassemia trait, confirmed by hemoglobin electrophoresis with elevated hemoglobin A2.

subtopic: Brachial plexus — upper trunk lesion
vignette: A 24-year-old man is evaluated after a motorcycle collision in which his right shoulder was driven forcefully downward. On examination, the right arm hangs adducted and internally rotated at the side, and the forearm is pronated and extended. He is unable to abduct the arm at the shoulder, externally rotate it, supinate the forearm, or flex the elbow. Sensation is diminished over the lateral shoulder and the lateral forearm. Reflexes at the biceps and brachioradialis are absent, but the triceps reflex is preserved. Hand intrinsic muscle strength and grip are intact.
leadIn: Which structure was most likely injured?

options.a: Upper trunk of the brachial plexus
options.b: Superior trunk of the brachial plexus
options.c: Lateral cord of the brachial plexus
options.d: C5 nerve root
options.e: Posterior cord of the brachial plexus

explanation: The pattern of motor loss — absent shoulder abduction, external rotation, elbow flexion, and forearm supination — reflects injury to the C5 and C6 contributions before they divide into anterior and posterior divisions. **The upper trunk of the brachial plexus** carries exactly these combined fibres, and its injury produces the classic **Erb-Duchenne palsy** ("waiter's tip" position). A single root lesion would not simultaneously abolish both biceps and brachioradialis reflexes while sparing all hand function; a cord lesion would additionally disrupt either median or radial downstream branches.

distractorExplanations.b: A C6 root lesion alone would affect biceps and brachioradialis reflexes but would spare most deltoid and infraspinatus function, which are predominantly C5.
distractorExplanations.c: The lateral cord gives rise to the musculocutaneous and lateral median nerves; a lesion here would weaken elbow flexion and forearm flexion but would spare the posterior cord muscles responsible for shoulder abduction and external rotation.
distractorExplanations.d: A C5 root lesion alone would weaken shoulder abduction and external rotation but would not fully abolish elbow flexion and supination, which depend heavily on C6 contribution to the musculocutaneous nerve.
distractorExplanations.e: The posterior cord gives rise to the axillary and radial nerves; a lesion here would abolish shoulder abduction and extension but would spare elbow flexion and supination carried by the musculocutaneous nerve.

teachingPoint: Erb-Duchenne palsy results from upper trunk (C5–C6) injury, classically from downward traction on the shoulder. The arm adducts and internally rotates (loss of deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus), the elbow extends and the forearm pronates (loss of biceps and supinator), producing the waiter's tip posture. The key anatomical reasoning is that only a trunk-level lesion combines C5 and C6 deficits before anterior/posterior division, while sparing lower trunk hand function.

subtopic: Aortic Stenosis — Referred for Valve Replacement
vignette: A 76-year-old man is evaluated for 6 months of progressive shortness of breath when climbing stairs and two episodes of near-syncope while walking uphill. He has smoked half a pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years. On examination, BP is 145/85 mm Hg and pulse is 78/min and regular. options.c: Repeat echocardiography in 6 to 12 months
options.d: Refer for percutaneous balloon aortic valvuloplasty
options.e: Refer for aortic valve replacement

subtopic: Mature cystic teratoma (dermoid cyst) — histologic identification
vignette: A 26-year-old woman undergoes a laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy for a 4-cm cyst that was incidentally found on a pelvic ultrasound. On gross examination, the cystic mass contains a thick yellow material, hair, and a well-formed tooth. Microscopic sections show a cyst wall lined by squamous epithelium with underlying sebaceous glands, hair follicles, and a focus of thyroid tissue.
leadIn: The presence of tissue from all three germ cell layers in this neoplasm is most consistent with which of the following origins?

options.a: Ovarian surface epithelium
options.b: Primordial germ cell
options.c: Ovarian stromal cell
options.d: Mesothelial cell
options.e: Embryonic germ cell precursor

explanation: The gross findings of hair, teeth, and sebaceous material are pathognomonic for a **mature cystic teratoma (dermoid cyst)**, the most common ovarian germ cell tumor. These tumors arise from a single **primordial germ cell** and contain differentiated tissue from all three germ layers: ectoderm (squamous epithelium, hair, teeth), mesoderm (muscle, bone), and endoderm (thyroid tissue, gastrointestinal epithelium). The presence of thyroid tissue specifically confirms the inclusion of endodermal derivatives.

distractorExplanations.a: Ovarian surface epithelium gives rise to serous and mucinous cystadenomas, which do not contain tissue from multiple germ layers.
distractorExplanations.c: Ovarian stromal cells give rise to sex cord-stromal tumors such as fibromas and granulosa cell tumors, not teratomas.
distractorExplanations.d: Mesothelial cells are the origin of ovarian surface epithelial tumors, not germ cell tumors.
distractorExplanations.e: Endodermal sinus cells are associated with yolk sac tumors, which produce alpha-fetoprotein and do not contain mature tissue from all three germ layers.

teachingPoint: Mature cystic teratomas are the most common ovarian germ cell tumor, arising from primordial germ cells. They characteristically contain tissue from all three germ layers, with ectodermal elements (hair, teeth, sebaceous glands) being most prominent. A rare complication is struma ovarii, in which thyroid tissue is the predominant component and can cause hyperthyroidism.

He has chronic ascites managed with spironolactone and furosemide. His temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 104/min, respiratory rate is 22/min, blood pressure is 104/62 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 91% on room air. Examination shows scleral icterus, distended abdomen with shifting dullness, and absent breath sounds over the lower third of the right hemithorax with stony dullness to percussion. Chest radiograph shows a large right pleural effusion without an infiltrate. Diagnostic thoracentesis yields straw-colored fluid with a protein of 1.8 g/dL (serum protein 5.6 g/dL), LDH of 110 U/L (serum LDH 240 U/L), pH of 7.40, glucose of 88 mg/dL, and 900 neutrophils/µL; Gram stain shows gram-negative rods. Ascitic fluid analysis shows 420 neutrophils/µL.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.a: Oral levofloxacin with outpatient follow-up in 48 hours
options.b: Intravenous cefotaxime plus tube thoracostomy drainage
options.c: Treatment with intravenous ceftriaxone alone
options.d: Large-volume paracentesis and thoracentesis alone
options.e: Intravenous cefotaxime alone

explanation: This patient with cirrhosis and a chronic **hepatic hydrothorax** has developed **spontaneous bacterial empyema**, the pleural-space counterpart of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis: the fluid is infected by translocation of gut bacteria, here evidenced by gram-negative rods and a neutrophil count above 250 cells/µL despite the fluid remaining transudate-like by protein and LDH. In cirrhotic hydrothorax, a low-protein, low-LDH fluid does not exclude infection, so neutrophil counts and Gram stain drive the diagnosis. Management mirrors spontaneous bacterial peritonitis: broad beta-lactam therapy such as **intravenous cefotaxime**, plus **albumin** for renal protection in advanced cirrhosis, without tube drainage. Chest tubes are specifically avoided in spontaneous bacterial empyema because continuous drainage of a cirrhotic patient's protein-rich fluid causes severe protein depletion, electrolyte imbalance, and sepsis without improving outcomes.

distractorExplanations.a: Spontaneous bacterial empyema carries high mortality in advanced cirrhosis and requires inpatient parenteral therapy; oral outpatient therapy is inadequate.
distractorExplanations.b: The antibiotic choice is right, but adding a chest tube applies the parapneumonic-effusion rule to the wrong disease; tube drainage in cirrhotic hydrothorax causes life-threatening protein and electrolyte loss.
distractorExplanations.c: Anaerobic coverage is unnecessary for enteric gram-negative translocation, and the chest tube carries the same harm as in option b.
distractorExplanations.d: Draining fluid without antibiotics fails to treat the bacteremia-driving translocation, and the infection will recur immediately.

teachingPoint: Spontaneous bacterial empyema (infected hepatic hydrothorax, neutrophils >250/µL) is treated with antibiotics alone — chest tube drainage is contraindicated because it depletes protein in a cirrhotic patient.
reviewerFlag: Neutrophil threshold >250/µL for spontaneous bacterial empyema parallels the SBP criterion and is standard teaching; guideline from memory, unconfirmed. Albumin co-administration in SBE is extrapolated from SBP practice and is not tested in the options.
change: option c paraphrases the key

subtopic: Potassium shifts in DKA
vignette: A 24-year-old man with type 1 diabetes presents with fatigue, polyuria, and Kussmaul respirations. His blood glucose is 410 mg/dL, arterial pH is 7.28, and serum potassium is 5.8 mEq/L despite a report of poor oral intake for two days. The total body potassium stores in this patient are significantly depleted.
leadIn: Which of the following mechanisms most directly explains the elevation of his serum potassium despite total body potassium depletion?

options.a: Impaired function of the Na+/K+-ATPase pump in skeletal muscle
options.b: Increased urinary potassium excretion from aldosterone activation
options.c: Inhibition of the Na+/K+-ATPase in skeletal muscle
options.d: Massive intravascular hemolysis releasing intracellular potassium
options.e: Suppression of the Na+/K+-ATPase in the proximal renal tubule

explanation: Insulin normally stimulates the **Na+/K+-ATPase** pump on cell membranes, driving potassium from the extracellular fluid into cells. In DKA, **absolute insulin deficiency** removes this stimulus, causing potassium to shift out of cells into the serum. Concurrent **acidosis** further promotes extracellular potassium shift via intracellular H+ buffering. This produces hyperkalemia even though total body potassium is depleted from osmotic diuresis.

distractorExplanations.a: Activation of the Na+/K+-ATPase would drive potassium intracellularly, producing hypokalemia rather than hyperkalemia.
distractorExplanations.b: Aldosterone does promote urinary potassium loss, but this mechanism explains the total body depletion, not the elevated serum concentration.
distractorExplanations.d: Hemolysis can elevate serum potassium, but there is no clinical evidence of hemolysis in this presentation.
distractorExplanations.e: The Na+/K+-ATPase in the proximal tubule is not the primary determinant of the acute transcellular potassium shift seen in DKA; the major shift occurs in skeletal muscle and liver.

teachingPoint: Hyperkalemia in DKA is a distributional phenomenon caused by insulin deficiency and acidosis driving potassium extracellularly; it masks profound total body potassium depletion.
change: option a paraphrases the key

subtopic: Ductal-dependent critical coarctation in the neonate
vignette: A male infant is born at 39 weeks' gestation by spontaneous vaginal delivery; birth weight is 3.3 kg and Apgar scores are 8 and 9. He is discharged home on day 2 of life feeding well. On day 4 he is brought to the emergency department with poor feeding, rapid breathing, and lethargy. Temperature is 36.4°C, pulse is 186/min, respirations are 72/min, and blood pressure is 62/38 mm Hg in the right arm. He is pale and mottled with weak peripheral pulses overall; femoral pulses are impalpable while brachial pulses remain palpable. There is no murmur. The liver edge is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin. Capillary refill is 5 seconds. Laboratory studies show pH 7.18, bicarbonate 12 mEq/L, and lactate 7.8 mmol/L. Chest radiograph shows cardiomegaly with pulmonary venous congestion. Blood cultures are drawn and empiric antibiotics are started.
leadIn: In addition to intravenous fluids and inotropic support, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.a: Indomethacin intravenous administration
options.b: Prostacyclin continuous infusion
options.c: Alprostadil continuous infusion
options.d: Milrinone intravenous infusion
options.e: Prostaglandin E1 continuous infusion

explanation: A newborn who is well for the first 2 days and then collapses into **shock with absent femoral pulses and severe metabolic acidosis** has a **ductal-dependent obstructive left-heart lesion**, most commonly **critical coarctation of the aorta**: the descending aorta is perfused through the ductus arteriosus, and spontaneous ductal closure on day 2 to 3 precipitates cardiovascular collapse. The murmur is absent because the lesion itself is silent in the newborn. The immediate priority is to **reopen and maintain the ductus arteriosus with a prostaglandin E1 infusion**, which restores lower-body perfusion and allows stabilization before definitive surgical repair.

distractorExplanations.a: Indomethacin closes the ductus arteriosus; in this infant the ductus is the only route supplying the descending aorta, so closing it would be fatal.
distractorExplanations.b: Prostacyclin is a pulmonary and systemic vasodilator used in persistent pulmonary hypertension; it does not reopen the ductus arteriosus and would worsen systemic hypotension.
distractorExplanations.c: Definitive surgical repair is required, but the infant must first be stabilized with prostaglandin E1 and metabolic resuscitation; taking an unstable, acidotic neonate directly to the operating room is not the next step.
distractorExplanations.d: Milrinone may lower afterload but does nothing for the anatomic obstruction or the ductal dependency that caused the collapse.

teachingPoint: A well newborn who collapses into shock at 2-3 days of life has ductal closure unmasking a ductal-dependent lesion; absent femoral pulses point to critical coarctation, and the immediate step is prostaglandin E1 to reopen the ductus.
change: option c paraphrases the key

subtopic: Coronary anatomy and conduction system
vignette: A 68-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after the onset of crushing substernal chest pain radiating to his left arm. He is diaphoretic and nauseated. Blood pressure is 148/90 mm Hg and pulse is irregular at 44/min. ECG shows ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. Serum troponin I is pending.
leadIn: Occlusion of which vascular structure is the most likely cause of his bradyarrhythmia?

options.a: AV nodal branch of the left circumflex artery
options.b: First septal perforating branch of the left anterior descending artery
options.c: Posterior descending branch of the left circumflex artery
options.d: Atrioventricular nodal artery originating from the right coronary artery
options.e: AV nodal branch of the right coronary artery

explanation: ST elevation in leads **II, III, and aVF** localizes the infarct to the **inferior wall**, supplied by the **right coronary artery** in the large majority of patients. The RCA also gives off the branch that supplies the **AV node**, so inferior infarcts commonly produce AV nodal conduction abnormalities such as Mobitz I block, which explains his irregular bradycardia.

distractorExplanations.a: The left circumflex supplies the lateral wall and can give rise to the AV nodal branch in a minority of patients, but the inferior ECG localization points to the RCA territory.
distractorExplanations.b: Septal perforators of the LAD supply the anteroseptal wall and bundle branches; occlusion there produces anterior ST elevation, not inferior changes.
distractorExplanations.c: The posterior descending artery arises from the RCA in most patients, but it supplies the posterior wall and does not perfuse the AV node.
distractorExplanations.d: A circumflex-origin sinus node branch could cause sinus bradycardia, but the inferior ST elevation indicates an RCA lesion, and his rhythm is consistent with AV nodal block.

teachingPoint: Inferior STEMI (II, III, aVF) = RCA occlusion; the RCA supplies the SA node in 60% and the AV node in 80-90% of patients, so bradyarrhythmias and AV block are common.
reviewerFlag: Percentages for SA/AV nodal supply are quoted from memory; reviewer should confirm exact figures (commonly cited as SA node 60% RCA, AV node 80-90% RCA).
change: option d paraphrases the key

subtopic: Fabry disease — lysosomal Gb3 deposition causing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
vignette: A 26-year-old man is evaluated for progressive shortness of breath on exertion over the past year. Since childhood he has had recurrent episodes of burning pain in his hands and feet triggered by heat and exercise, which were attributed to a nerve problem. He reports decreased sweating. Examination shows multiple dark red punctate vascular lesions on his lower abdomen and scrotum. Urinalysis shows 2+ protein. Transthoracic echocardiography shows concentric left ventricular wall thickening with diastolic dysfunction; the walls have a speckled, ground-glass appearance on the echogenicity images. Serum leukocyte alpha-galactosidase A activity is markedly reduced. His maternal uncle died of heart failure at age 42.
leadIn: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of this patient's cardiomyopathy?

options.a: Deposition of insoluble fibrillar proteins in the extracellular matrix with amyloid-positive Congo red staining
options.b: Iron deposition within myocardial cells with reactive oxidative injury and fibrosis
options.c: Accumulation of globotriaosylceramide within lysosomes of myocardial cells
options.d: Buildup of glycosphingolipid substrate within intracellular lysosomal compartments of cardiac myocytes
options.e: Sarcomere protein mutation causing myocyte disarray with asymmetric septal hypertrophy

explanation: This patient has **Fabry disease**, an **X-linked lysosomal storage disorder** caused by deficiency of **alpha-galactosidase A**. Because the deficient enzyme normally cleaves the terminal galactose from **globotriaosylceramide (Gb3)**, the substrate accumulates within lysosomes of endothelial, renal, and cardiac cells. The cardiac consequence is **Gb3 accumulation within lysosomes of myocardial cells**, which produces concentric hypertrophy with a characteristic speckled, ground-glass appearance on echocardiography and eventual diastolic dysfunction. The other features anchor the diagnosis: heat-triggered neuropathic pain, hypohidrosis, **angiokeratomas**, and proteinuria from renal deposition.

distractorExplanations.a: Amyloid deposition, as in AL or transthyretin amyloidosis, produces a restrictive cardiomyopathy with Congo red–positive extracellular fibrils, not lysosomal storage; the reduced alpha-galactosidase A activity excludes it.
distractorExplanations.b: Iron deposition from hereditary hemochromatosis can cause a dilated or restrictive cardiomyopathy, but it does not cause neuropathic pain, angiokeratomas, or reduced alpha-galactosidase A activity.
distractorExplanations.d: Viral myocarditis causes a dilated cardiomyopathy with lymphocytic infiltration and elevated troponin, not concentric hypertrophy with a storage-disorder phenotype.
distractorExplanations.e: A sarcomere protein mutation causes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with asymmetric septal hypertrophy and myocyte disarray, which does not fit the lysosomal enzyme deficiency or the systemic findings here.

teachingPoint: Fabry disease — X-linked alpha-galactosidase A deficiency — causes globotriaosylceramide to accumulate in myocardial lysosomes, producing concentric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with a speckled, ground-glass echocardiographic appearance.
reviewerFlag: The speckled ground-glass echocardiographic appearance of Fabry cardiomyopathy is from memory, unconfirmed.
change: option d paraphrases the key

subtopic: Urea cycle — carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I deficiency
vignette: A 2-day-old girl is evaluated in the neonatal intensive care unit for hypothermia, poor feeding, and progressive obtundation. She was born at term, and the pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated. She fed well on the first day of life but became lethargic and stopped latching yesterday. On examination she is hypotonic, minimally responsive, and has a normal fontanelle without dysmorphic features. Laboratory studies show a plasma ammonia of 610 μmol/L with normal glucose, normal lactate, no anion-gap acidosis, and no ketones. Urine organic acid screening detects no orotic acid. Quantitative plasma amino acids show a citrulline concentration below the detectable limit.
leadIn: Which enzyme is most likely deficient in this infant?

options.a: The mitochondrial enzyme that catalyzes the synthesis of carbamoyl phosphate from ammonia and bicarbonate
options.b: Arginase
options.c: Argininosuccinate synthetase
options.d: Argininosuccinate lyase
options.e: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I

explanation: The first step of the **urea cycle** is the mitochondrial condensation of ammonia and bicarbonate into carbamoyl phosphate, catalyzed by **carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I**, which requires **N-acetylglutamate** as an obligate allosteric activator. When CPS1 is deficient, carbamoyl phosphate is never made, so no orotic acid appears in the urine — the opposite of ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, where carbamoyl phosphate accumulates and spills into pyrimidine synthesis. The undetectable citrulline is consistent: without carbamoyl phosphate, citrulline cannot be formed, distinguishing this from the citrullinemias, in which citrulline is markedly elevated.

distractorExplanations.a: Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency would also cause neonatal hyperammonemia, but carbamoyl phosphate is produced and diverted to pyrimidine synthesis, producing orotic aciduria that is absent here.
distractorExplanations.b: Arginase deficiency presents later in childhood with spastic diplegia and elevated arginine, not with undetectable citrulline and neonatal coma.
distractorExplanations.c: Argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency causes citrulline to accumulate to very high levels rather than disappear, so the undetectable citrulline excludes it.
distractorExplanations.d: Argininosuccinate lyase deficiency produces elevated citrulline and urinary argininosuccinic acid, neither of which is present in this infant.

teachingPoint: In neonatal hyperammonemia, orotic aciduria separates OTC deficiency (present) from CPS1 deficiency (absent); a citrulline level then separates CPS1 deficiency (undetectable) from the citrullinemias (markedly elevated).
reviewerFlag: System overlap: urea cycle is biochemistry content, outside the Hematology & Oncology brief; generated per requested topic and flagged. Content is standard Step 1 biochemistry.
change: option a paraphrases the key

subtopic: Knee dislocation — vascular injury and imaging
vignette: A 28-year-old man is brought to the trauma bay after a high-speed motor vehicle collision in which his knee struck the dashboard. He reports severe right knee pain. Blood pressure is 134/82 mmHg, heart rate 96 bpm. The right knee is grossly deformed with posterior displacement of the tibia relative to the femur. Distal pulses are palpable but diminished. Doppler examination reveals an ankle-brachial index of 0.82 on the right and 1.04 on the left. Sensation is intact throughout the right leg. The knee is splinted and reduced with inline traction, and post-reduction radiographs confirm congruent reduction.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.a: CT angiogram of the right lower extremity
options.b: Admit for serial ABI measurements every 4 hours for 24 hours
options.c: Emergent surgical exploration of the popliteal artery
options.d: Conventional angiography in the interventional radiology suite
options.e: Obtain a contrast-enhanced CT study of the vessels of the right leg

explanation: Posterior knee dislocation from a dashboard mechanism carries a high rate of **popliteal artery injury** because the vessel is tethered behind the tibia and cannot tolerate the posterior displacement force. Although distal pulses are present, the **ABI of 0.82** is abnormal (below the 0.9 threshold), which mandates vascular imaging. **CT angiography** is the current first-line study because it is rapidly available, noninvasive, and highly sensitive for intimal injuries, pseudoaneurysms, and thromboses that may not be apparent on physical examination alone. An initially normal pulse exam does not exclude a popliteal intimal tear, which can progress to delayed thrombosis and limb-threatening ischemia.

distractorExplanations.b: Serial ABI monitoring is appropriate only when the ABI is normal (≥0.9) after reduction; an abnormal ABI mandates immediate imaging.
distractorExplanations.c: Emergent surgical exploration is reserved for signs of limb ischemia — absent pulses, a cold pale foot, or an expanding hematoma — not for an abnormal ABI alone, which first requires imaging to localize the injury.
distractorExplanations.d: Conventional angiography offers excellent imaging but is less readily available, more invasive, and slower to obtain than CT angiography, which is now preferred for initial evaluation.
distractorExplanations.e: Discharge is contraindicated after knee dislocation with an abnormal ABI; occult vascular injury can progress to limb-threatening ischemia.

teachingPoint: Any knee dislocation with ABI < 0.9 mandates CT angiography, even if distal pulses are palpable. Popliteal artery intimal injuries can progress to thrombosis with initially normal examinations.
change: option e paraphrases the key

subtopic: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy — sudden death prevention
vignette: A 24-year-old man is evaluated in cardiology clinic after an episode of syncope during a competitive basketball game. He lost consciousness for roughly 20 seconds while sprinting and awoke with confusion that cleared within a minute. He has had exertional dyspnea for the past year but no chest pain. His father died suddenly at age 34 while swimming; an autopsy was never performed. He takes no medications and does not smoke. Blood pressure is 124/72 mmHg and pulse is 62/min. Cardiac examination reveals a harsh systolic ejection murmur at the left sternal border that increases with standing and decreases with squatting; the remainder of the examination is normal. ECG shows deep T-wave inversions in the lateral precordial leads. Echocardiography demonstrates asymmetric septal hypertrophy with a maximal wall thickness of 20 mm, systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve, and a resting left ventricular outflow tract gradient of 60 mmHg; ejection fraction is 68%. He is started on a beta blocker and counseled to avoid competitive athletics.
leadIn: In addition to the beta blocker and activity restriction, which of the following is the most appropriate next step to reduce this patient's risk of death?

options.a: Subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator implantation
options.b: Placement of a subcutaneous ICD
options.c: Permanent pacemaker implantation for syncope prevention
options.d: Septal myectomy to relieve the outflow tract gradient
options.e: Amiodarone therapy for ventricular arrhythmia suppression

explanation: This patient has obstructive **hypertrophic cardiomyopathy**, and his syncope on exertion plus a **family history of sudden cardiac death** place him at high risk for **sudden cardiac death** from ventricular arrhythmia. The intervention shown to reduce mortality in high-risk HCM patients is an **implantable cardioverter-defibrillator**, which terminates the ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation that causes these events. Beta blockers and activity restriction address symptoms and exposure, but they do not protect against an arrhythmic arrest; the defibrillator does. Septal reduction is reserved for patients with refractory symptoms despite maximally tolerated medical therapy, and this patient has only New York Heart Association class II symptoms at first presentation.

distractorExplanations.b: Transplantation is considered only for end-stage HCM with refractory heart failure or intractable arrhythmias despite maximal therapy, not at first presentation with preserved systolic function.
distractorExplanations.c: Pacing does not prevent sudden arrhythmic death; it is indicated for conduction disease or bradyarrhythmias, neither of which this patient has.
distractorExplanations.d: Septal myectomy or alcohol ablation improves symptoms and gradient in patients refractory to medical therapy, but gradient reduction has not been established to reduce sudden death risk the way defibrillator implantation has.
distractorExplanations.e: Amiodarone can reduce arrhythmia burden but has not been shown to reduce sudden death risk in HCM and carries substantial long-term toxicity; it does not substitute for defibrillator protection.

teachingPoint: HCM + exertional syncope or family history of sudden death = high sudden-death risk → implantable cardioverter-defibrillator, regardless of symptom therapy.
reviewerFlag: From memory, unconfirmed: ICD indication in HCM based on major risk factors (syncope, family history of sudden death, wall thickness ≥30 mm) — current ESC/ACC-AHA guidance supports defibrillator implantation for patients judged at high risk; exact risk-factor weighting should be verified against the current guideline.
change: option b paraphrases the key

subtopic: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy — sudden death risk stratification and ICD indication
vignette: A 19-year-old collegiate rower is evaluated after an episode of loss of consciousness. He was completing an intense interval session when he felt lightheaded and collapsed; he woke within seconds on the dock without confusion or incontinence. He reports two similar episodes of near-syncope during hard training over the past four months, and occasional exertional chest tightness that resolves with rest. His father died unexpectedly at age 38 while playing basketball; an autopsy was never performed. On examination, vital signs are normal. Cardiac examination reveals a harsh systolic murmur at the left sternal border that intensifies when the patient performs a Valsalva maneuver and softens with passive leg elevation. The carotid upstrokes are brisk. An ECG shows deep T-wave inversions in the lateral precordial leads and prominent septal Q waves. Echocardiography reports asymmetric septal hypertrophy with a resting left ventricular outflow tract gradient of 25 mm Hg and normal systolic function.
leadIn: In addition to activity restriction, which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient?

options.a: Insertion of an implantable defibrillator
options.b: Initiation of oral amiodarone therapy
options.c: Septal myectomy without device therapy
options.d: Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement
options.e: Alcohol septal ablation without device therapy

explanation: Exertional syncope in a young athlete with a **murmur that intensifies with Valsalva** and asymmetric septal hypertrophy establishes **hypertrophic cardiomyopathy** with dynamic outflow tract obstruction. The decision this patient forces is sudden-death prevention, and he carries two major risk factors: **unexplained syncope during exertion** and a **family history of sudden cardiac death** before age 50. Because these risk factors place him at high enough risk for ventricular arrhythmia, the guideline-supported intervention is **implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement** as primary prevention. Medication and septal reduction therapy address the gradient and symptoms, but they do not protect against the arrhythmic event that killed his father.

distractorExplanations.a: Delaying risk management for surveillance would leave a high-risk patient unprotected; his risk factors justify device therapy now, not further observation.
distractorExplanations.b: Amiodarone suppresses atrial and ventricular ectopy, but it has never been shown to prevent sudden death in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and is not a substitute for device therapy in a high-risk patient.
distractorExplanations.c: Septal myectomy relieves outflow obstruction and symptoms but does not reduce the risk of ventricular fibrillation, which is the threat signaled by his syncope and family history.
distractorExplanations.e: Alcohol septal ablation reduces the gradient but creates scar that can itself be arrhythmogenic, and like myectomy it does not address his sudden-death risk.

teachingPoint: In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, exertional syncope plus a family history of sudden cardiac death are major sudden-death risk factors; the intervention that addresses that risk is an ICD, not gradient-reducing therapy.
reviewerFlag: ICD indication for HCM is based on an individualized risk score; exertional syncope and family history of SCD are established major risk factors driving device decisions in most guidelines. From memory, unconfirmed whether current ESC/ACC wording would mandate ICD for exactly two risk factors versus recommend it — flagged for reviewer.
change: option a paraphrases the key

subtopic: Pediatric renal tumors — Wilms tumor cell of origin
vignette: A 3-year-old girl is brought to her pediatrician because her mother noticed a fullness in her abdomen while bathing her. The child has been eating normally and has had no fevers or weight loss. Examination reveals a firm, smooth, non-tender mass in the left flank that does not cross the midline. Her blood pressure is 138/92 mmHg, and urinalysis shows 10–15 RBC/hpf with no casts. Serum LDH and vanillylmandelic acid are normal. Abdominal ultrasound shows a large renal mass with a pseudocapsule; a claw sign is noted at the renal pole.
leadIn: This tumor most likely arose from which of the following embryologic cells?

options.a: Metanephric mesenchymal progenitor cell
options.b: Metanephric blastema
options.c: Primitive neuroectodermal cell
options.d: Pluripotent embryonal cell of the gonad
options.e: Hepatoblast precursor

explanation: A painless flank mass with **hypertension**, hematuria, and a **claw sign** on ultrasound in a young child is classic for **Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma)**. The hypertension reflects renin secretion by the tumor. Wilms tumor arises from persistent **metanephric blastema** — the primitive metanephric mesenchyme that normally differentiates into mature nephrons — and is associated with loss of **WT1**, as seen in WAGR and Denys-Drash syndromes. Failure of these embryonal renal precursors to mature leaves nests of blastemal cells (nephrogenic rests) that can proliferate into a triphasic tumor containing blastema, stroma, and epithelium.

distractorExplanations.a: The neural crest sympathoadrenal precursor gives rise to neuroblastoma, which typically crosses the midline, secretes catecholamines (elevated VMA/HVA), and causes fever and weight loss — the normal VMA here argues against it.
distractorExplanations.c: Primitive neuroectodermal cells give rise to tumors such as medulloblastoma and Ewing sarcoma, not renal masses.
distractorExplanations.d: Pluripotent embryonal cells of the gonad give rise to germ cell tumors such as yolk sac tumor and teratoma, which arise in the gonads or midline, not in the kidney.
distractorExplanations.e: Hepatoblast precursors give rise to hepatoblastoma, an infantile liver tumor presenting with a right upper quadrant mass and often elevated alpha-fetoprotein.

teachingPoint: Wilms tumor = nephroblastoma from metanephric blastema, associated with WT1 loss (WAGR, Denys-Drash, Beckwith-Wiedemann). Wilms: age ~3, hypertension, hematuria, claw sign. Neuroblastoma: age <2, sympathetic chain, catecholamines, crosses midline.
reviewerFlag: Buzzword 'claw sign' is used from memory; confident it is a recognized First Aid/UWorld descriptor for Wilms tumor on imaging.
change: option a paraphrases the key

subtopic: Post-MI ventricular arrhythmia and ICD indication
vignette: A 59-year-old man is recovering in the coronary care unit on hospital day 2 after an anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction, treated with primary angioplasty and stenting of a proximal left anterior descending occlusion. He has been free of chest pain since reperfusion. This morning, telemetry captures a 30-second run of monomorphic ventricular tachycardia at 160/min; his blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg and he is asymptomatic, and the rhythm terminates spontaneously. He is already receiving aspirin, ticagrelor, metoprolol, lisinopril, and atorvastatin. An echocardiogram obtained this morning shows an ejection fraction of 28% with anterior akinesis. Serum potassium is 4.0 mEq/L and magnesium is 2.0 mg/dL; troponin is falling appropriately.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate management of this patient's arrhythmia?

options.a: Reassessment of ejection fraction at least 40 days after the infarct
options.b: Immediate electrophysiology study with ablation
options.c: Repeat evaluation of left ventricular systolic function no sooner than 40 days post-infarction
options.d: Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement before discharge
options.e: Lidocaine infusion for 48 hours

explanation: Ventricular tachycardia within the first 48 hours after an acute infarct reflects the **electrical instability of the acutely injured myocardium** and does not by itself establish an ICD indication. The decision that matters is what happens once the myocardium has had time to recover: guidelines require **reassessment of ejection fraction at least 40 days post-MI on optimal medical therapy**, because **stunned myocardium** frequently recovers function, and an ICD implanted too early exposes patients to device complications without benefit. If the EF remains ≤35% at that reassessment, primary-prevention ICD implantation is indicated. His hemodynamically tolerated, self-terminating run needs continued beta blockade and electrolyte vigilance, not an acute intervention.

distractorExplanations.b: Electrophysiology study with ablation is reserved for recurrent sustained VT unresponsive to therapy or specific substrates; a single self-terminating run on day 2 does not warrant this.
distractorExplanations.c: Lifelong amiodarone does not improve mortality in this setting and adds pulmonary, thyroid, and hepatic toxicity; beta blockade is the antiarrhythmic backbone after MI.
distractorExplanations.d: ICD implantation within 40 days of an MI is not indicated even with a low ejection fraction, because recovery of stunned myocardium may eliminate the need and early devices carry harm without proven benefit.
distractorExplanations.e: Prophylactic lidocaine was abandoned decades ago because it increased mortality from asystole despite suppressing ventricular ectopy.

teachingPoint: VT within 48 hours of acute MI is treated acutely but does not mandate an ICD. Reassess EF at ≥40 days post-MI on optimal medical therapy; implant an ICD for primary prevention only if EF remains ≤35%.
reviewerFlag: The 40-day post-MI ICD waiting period and EF ≤35% threshold are established guideline values from memory; reviewer should confirm currency.
change: option c paraphrases the key

subtopic: Chagas myocarditis — histologic finding
vignette: A 52-year-old man from rural Brazil is evaluated for progressive dyspnea and leg swelling over the past year. He has had longstanding difficulty swallowing and chronic constipation. Examination shows jugular venous distention, bibasilar crackles, an S3 gallop, and pitting edema of both legs. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 28% and a small apical aneurysm. Endomyocardial biopsy shows a lymphocytic infiltrate in the myocardium, and a peripheral smear and serology are pending. Colon imaging shows a markedly dilated sigmoid colon.
leadIn: Which of the following histologic findings is most likely to be present on examination of this patient's myocardial tissue?

options.a: Intracellular protozoal parasites forming cystic structures inside cardiac muscle cells
options.b: Multinucleated giant cells with eosinophilic necrosis
options.c: Amastigote-filled pseudocysts within cardiac myocytes
options.d: Fibrinous pericardial exudate with frond-like projections
options.e: Intranuclear viral inclusion bodies with myocyte necrosis

explanation: The combination of a **dilated cardiomyopathy with an apical aneurysm**, GI dysmotility (dysphagia and megacolon), and residence in **rural Latin America** identifies chronic **Chagas disease** caused by *Trypanosoma cruzi*. In infected myocardium, the parasite replicates intracellularly, producing **amastigote-filled pseudocysts within cardiac myocytes** surrounded by a lymphocytic infiltrate — the specific finding that distinguishes Chagas myocarditis from other causes of dilated cardiomyopathy.

distractorExplanations.a: Caseating granulomas suggest tuberculosis or fungal infection, neither of which explains the megacolon and apical aneurysm in this epidemiologic setting.
distractorExplanations.b: Multinucleated giant cells with eosinophilic necrosis characterize giant cell myocarditis, a rapidly progressive disease of younger patients without the GI features of this case.
distractorExplanations.d: A fibrinous pericardial exudate would indicate uremic or viral pericarditis and would not cause the dilated cardiomyopathy or megacolon described.
distractorExplanations.e: Viral inclusions with myocyte necrosis would suggest cytomegalovirus or adenovirus myocarditis, which is acute and lacks the chronic GI dysmotility and apical aneurysm.

teachingPoint: Chronic Chagas disease causes dilated cardiomyopathy with apical aneurysm plus megacolon/megaesophagus; cardiac histology shows amastigote-filled pseudocysts within myocytes.

subtopic: Ring-enhancing brain lesion — incomplete consent for stereotactic biopsy
vignette: A 41-year-old man with HIV and a last CD4 count of 45 cells/mm³ presents with two weeks of progressive left arm weakness and a dull right frontal headache. He is not taking antiretroviral therapy. On examination he has a left pronator drift and mild left-sided hyperreflexia. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain shows a single 3-cm ring-enhancing lesion in the right frontal lobe with surrounding oedema and mild midline shift. Toxoplasma IgG is positive. The neurosurgeon recommends stereotactic brain biopsy and says: "A small sample of the lesion will tell us whether this is an infection or a lymphoma, so we can treat you with the right drugs instead of guessing. The main risks are bleeding into the lesion or new weakness in your left arm. If you prefer, we can start empiric toxoplasmosis therapy and repeat the scan in two weeks instead of operating, and see whether the lesion shrinks."
leadIn: Which element of the BRAN framework has not yet been addressed in this discussion?

options.a: The benefits of the procedure
options.b: The consequences of declining all treatment
options.c: The alternatives to the procedure
options.d: The risks of the procedure
options.e: What could happen if he declines both the biopsy and the empiric medical therapy

explanation: The surgeon has explicitly covered three elements: the **benefits** (a tissue diagnosis distinguishing toxoplasmosis from lymphoma, so treatment is aimed at the right disease), the **risks** (haemorrhage into the lesion, new left arm weakness from the biopsy trajectory), and the **alternatives** (empiric toxoplasmosis therapy with repeat MRI in two weeks — the standard non-operative pathway when toxoplasma IgG is positive). What has not been discussed is the **'Nothing' element**: what happens if the patient declines both biopsy and all treatment — namely progressive mass effect, herniation risk and death from an untreated lesion. Until that is covered, the patient cannot weigh doing nothing against the options presented, and consent is incomplete.

distractorExplanations.a: The benefits were stated: tissue diagnosis that distinguishes infection from lymphoma and directs correct therapy.
distractorExplanations.c: The alternatives were stated: empiric toxoplasmosis therapy with repeat imaging rather than operation.
distractorExplanations.d: The risks were stated: bleeding into the lesion and new left arm weakness.
distractorExplanations.e: Both benefits and risks were explicitly discussed; the missing element is what happens if all intervention is declined.

teachingPoint: The 'Nothing' element of BRAN requires telling the patient what will happen if no procedure and no treatment are pursued — for a mass lesion with midline shift, that means progressive mass effect and the risk of herniation and death.

subtopic: Posterior shoulder dislocation evaluation
vignette: A 52-year-old man is evaluated in the emergency department 12 hours after a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. He complains of severe pain in both shoulders and is unable to actively raise either arm away from his side. He holds both arms splinted against his chest in adduction and internal rotation. Vital signs are within normal limits. Passive external rotation of either shoulder is sharply limited by pain and feels mechanically blocked. Standard anteroposterior radiographs of both shoulders are reported as showing no fracture and no definite dislocation, with the humeral heads appearing to sit normally over the glenoids. He has no prior history of shoulder injury or inflammatory arthritis. Neurovascular examination of both upper extremities is intact.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic study to confirm the suspected injury?

options.a: Axillary lateral radiographs of both shoulders
options.b: MRI of both shoulders without contrast
options.c: CT angiography of both shoulder girdles
options.d: Repeat anteroposterior radiographs in external rotation
options.e: Axillary view plain films of both shoulders

explanation: Generalized seizures produce violent **internal rotation and adduction** of the shoulder, a mechanism that classically causes **posterior shoulder dislocation**, often bilaterally. Posterior dislocations are easily missed on a single **AP radiograph** because the humeral head overlaps the glenoid in that plane and may appear normally located. The finding that the patient is **locked in internal rotation** and blocked on passive external rotation strongly suggests a posterior dislocation that the AP film failed to capture. An **axillary lateral view** visualizes the joint in the axial plane and directly demonstrates posterior displacement of the humeral head relative to the glenoid, making it the most appropriate next study.

distractorExplanations.b: MRI is useful for evaluating associated soft-tissue or labral injury but is not the first study to confirm a suspected posterior dislocation when standard radiography is equivocal.
distractorExplanations.c: CT angiography is indicated when a dislocation is associated with suspected vascular injury, but this patient's neurovascular examination is intact and the priority is to confirm the dislocation itself.
distractorExplanations.d: A repeat AP film, even in external rotation, does not reliably visualize posterior displacement in the axial plane and would not solve the diagnostic problem posed by the initial AP view.
distractorExplanations.e: Shoulder ultrasonography can detect some dislocations but is operator-dependent and does not provide the standardized osseous visualization needed to confirm posterior displacement and guide reduction.

teachingPoint: Posterior shoulder dislocation is a classic complication of seizure or electrocution and is frequently missed on standard AP radiographs. An axillary lateral or scapular Y view is required to confirm the diagnosis. A patient locked in internal rotation after a seizure should be assumed to have a posterior dislocation until proven otherwise.

subtopic: Acute upper GI bleeding — resuscitation and endoscopy timing
vignette: A 68-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after vomiting bright red blood and coffee-ground material at home, followed by a large black stool. He has a history of osteoarthritis, for which he takes ibuprofen 600 mg twice daily and low-dose aspirin 81 mg daily. He also takes metoprolol for hypertension. On arrival, he is pale and diaphoretic. Vital signs are blood pressure 84/52 mmHg, heart rate 128 bpm, respiratory rate 24, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. He is drowsy but arousable and answers questions appropriately. Abdominal examination reveals epigastric tenderness without guarding; rectal examination shows maroon-coloured stool. Two large-bore peripheral IV catheters are placed. Stat laboratory results are pending. The nurse asks what to do next.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate next step in this patient's management?

options.a: Administer IV omeprazole 80 mg bolus followed by 8 mg/hour infusion
options.b: Perform emergent upper endoscopy within 12 hours
options.c: Begin rapid isotonic crystalloid infusion and prepare for blood transfusion
options.d: Initiate aggressive volume resuscitation with isotonic fluids and cross-match blood for transfusion
options.e: Administer IV octreotide 50 mcg bolus followed by 50 mcg/hour infusion

explanation: This patient presents with **acute upper GI bleeding** (haematemesis and melena) in the setting of chronic NSAID and aspirin use, and he is in **haemorrhagic shock** (hypotension, tachycardia, altered mental status). The immediate priority in any unstable GI bleed is **volume resuscitation** with rapid isotonic crystalloid infusion and preparation for blood transfusion to restore tissue perfusion before any diagnostic or therapeutic intervention. Endoscopy within 12 hours, IV PPI infusion, and prokinetic agents all have roles in upper GI bleeding management, but they must follow initial resuscitation.

distractorExplanations.a: IV PPI infusion is part of upper GI bleeding management but is initiated after or alongside resuscitation, not before haemodynamic stability is achieved.
distractorExplanations.b: Emergent endoscopy within 12 hours is indicated for diagnosis and haemostasis but must follow initial stabilisation; performing endoscopy in an unstable, under-resuscitated patient increases procedural risk.
distractorExplanations.d: IV erythromycin improves gastric visualisation during endoscopy but is an adjunct given 30–90 minutes before the procedure, not the first intervention in a patient in haemorrhagic shock.
distractorExplanations.e: IV octreotide reduces splanchnic blood flow and is used when variceal bleeding is suspected, but this patient's NSAID use and epigastric tendibility favour a non-variceal source; regardless, resuscitation takes priority over any pharmacotherapy.

teachingPoint: In any patient presenting with acute GI bleeding and signs of **haemorrhagic shock** (hypotension, tachycardia, altered mental status), the first and most critical step is **volume resuscitation** with isotonic crystalloid and preparation for transfusion. All subsequent interventions — IV PPI infusion, octreotide for suspected variceal bleeding, erythromycin for endoscopic visualisation, and **urgent endoscopy within 12 hours** — must follow or accompany initial haemodynamic stabilisation, never precede it.

subtopic: Thyroid nodule — Bethesda VI, extent of surgery and neck dissection
vignette: A 47-year-old woman is evaluated for a 3.2-cm left thyroid nodule found on palpation during a routine physical. She has no history of head or neck irradiation and no family history of thyroid cancer. TSH is 2.4 mIU/L. Thyroid ultrasound shows a solid, hypoechoic 3.2-cm nodule in the left lobe with microcalcifications and irregular margins; no extrathyroidal extension is identified, and no contralateral thyroid nodules are present. No suspicious cervical lymph nodes are seen. Ultrasound-guided FNA cytology is diagnostic for papillary thyroid carcinoma (Bethesda VI).
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate surgical approach for this patient?

options.a: Total thyroidectomy with prophylactic bilateral central neck dissection
options.b: Left thyroid lobectomy alone
options.c: Diagnostic left thyroid lobectomy with intraoperative frozen section
options.d: Excision of the left thyroid lobe without any additional lymph node dissection
options.e: Total thyroidectomy with modified radical neck dissection

explanation: This patient has **Bethesda VI** cytology diagnostic for **papillary thyroid carcinoma**. The tumour is **<4 cm**, confined to one lobe with **no extrathyroidal extension**, no contralateral nodules, and no history of radiation — criteria that make **lobectomy** an adequate surgical extent rather than total thyroidectomy. The ultrasound shows **no suspicious lymphadenopathy**, and current guidelines do not mandate **prophylactic central neck dissection** for low-risk, clinically node-negative papillary thyroid carcinoma. Therefore lobectomy alone is the appropriate operation.

distractorExplanations.a: Total thyroidectomy with prophylactic central neck dissection is indicated for tumours >4 cm, extrathyroidal extension, or clinically apparent nodal disease; none of these are present, and overtreatment risks recurrent laryngeal nerve injury and hypoparathyroidism.
distractorExplanations.c: Frozen section is not routinely needed when cytology is already Bethesda VI; the diagnosis is established and the operation should proceed as a definitive lobectomy.
distractorExplanations.d: Prophylactic central neck dissection may be considered for higher-risk tumours or when nodal metastasis is suspected, but is not routinely indicated for a clinically node-negative low-risk papillary carcinoma <4 cm; adding it increases risk of hypoparathyroidism without proven benefit.
distractorExplanations.e: Modified radical neck dissection is reserved for confirmed lateral neck nodal metastasis (clinical N1b); there is no nodal disease here.

teachingPoint: Papillary thyroid carcinoma <4 cm, intrathyroidal, unilateral, with no nodal metastasis and no radiation history can be treated with lobectomy alone. Prophylactic central neck dissection is not routinely indicated for clinically node-negative low-risk disease.
reviewerFlag: Guideline from memory: ATA 2015 guidelines support lobectomy for papillary thyroid carcinoma 1–4 cm without extrathyroidal extension or nodal metastasis; prophylactic central neck dissection recommendation for low-risk clinically node-negative disease may vary by guideline update — confirm current ATA position.

subtopic: Cauda equina syndrome — recognition and imaging
vignette: A 52-year-old woman with a history of chronic low back pain presents to the emergency department with worsening lower back pain radiating to both legs over the past 24 hours. She also reports difficulty urinating for the past several hours. She has not had a bowel movement in two days. On examination, there is reduced strength in ankle dorsiflexion bilaterally. Pinprick sensation is diminished over the posterior thighs, perineum, and medial buttocks. A rectal exam reveals reduced anal sphincter tone. Knee reflexes are 2+ bilaterally; ankle reflexes are absent.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic study?

options.a: MRI of the lumbosacral spine without contrast
options.b: MRI of the lumbar spine with and without contrast
options.c: MRI of the lumbar spine without contrast
options.d: Plain radiographs of the lumbar spine
options.e: Electromyography and nerve conduction studies

explanation: This patient has **cauda equina syndrome**: bilateral radicular leg pain, **saddle anesthesia**, **urinary retention**, and reduced anal sphincter tone. The cauda equina contains the lumbosacral nerve roots, and compression below the L1–L2 level produces this constellation of findings. **Emergent MRI without contrast** of the lumbar spine is the study of choice to identify the level and cause of compression — most commonly a large central disc herniation — and to guide urgent surgical decompression.

distractorExplanations.a: CT of the lumbar spine can show bony pathology and acute hemorrhage but does not adequately visualize the nerve roots or a herniated disc compressing the cauda equina.
distractorExplanations.b: Contrast is unnecessary when the concern is a herniated disc or bony stenosis; contrast-enhanced MRI is reserved for suspected tumor, infection, or prior lumbar surgery.
distractorExplanations.d: Plain radiographs cannot visualize neural structures or disc tissue and have no role in the diagnosis of cauda equina compression.
distractorExplanations.e: Electrodiagnostic studies are used for chronic radicular or neuropathic evaluation over weeks to months and have no role in an acute myelopathic or cauda equina emergency.

teachingPoint: Cauda equina syndrome presents with bilateral leg pain, saddle anesthesia, urinary retention, and reduced anal sphincter tone. Emergent non-contrast MRI of the lumbar spine is the diagnostic study of choice to confirm compression and guide surgical decompression.
