subtopic: Hepatitis A — post-exposure prophylaxis
vignette: A woman calls the clinic 3 days after her roommate was diagnosed with acute hepatitis A. The roommate developed jaundice and was confirmed by IgM anti-HAV testing. The two share a bathroom and kitchen, and the patient helped care for her during the past week. The patient has never had hepatitis A and does not know whether she has been vaccinated. She has no jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, or fever today. Her immunization records cannot be located.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate management of this patient?

options.a: Hepatitis A vaccine and immune globulin
options.b: Immune globulin alone
options.c: Hepatitis A vaccine alone
options.d: Hepatitis A IgM antibody testing today
options.e: No prophylaxis; advise hand hygiene and return if symptomatic

explanation: This patient has a **household exposure to confirmed hepatitis A** within the past 2 weeks, the window in which **post-exposure prophylaxis** is effective. For healthy people aged 1 through 40 years, the recommended prophylaxis is the **hepatitis A vaccine alone**; immune globulin is added only for infants under 1 year, adults over 40, and patients who are **immunocompromised or have chronic liver disease**, because vaccine responses may be blunted in those groups. This patient is 26 and healthy, so vaccine alone is appropriate and also confers durable immunity against future exposures.

distractorExplanations.a: Combining vaccine with immune globulin is reserved for patients over 40, the immunocompromised, or those with chronic liver disease; in a healthy 26-year-old it unnecessarily reduces vaccine immunogenicity.
distractorExplanations.b: Immune globulin alone provides only temporary passive protection and is used when the patient cannot receive vaccine or is in a group with poor vaccine response.
distractorExplanations.d: IgM testing would only detect established infection; it does not address the need to prevent infection after a recent exposure.
distractorExplanations.e: Doing nothing forfeits the effective 2-week window for post-exposure prophylaxis in a clearly exposed household contact.

teachingPoint: After hepatitis A exposure, healthy people aged 1–40 receive the hepatitis A vaccine alone; add immune globulin for age >40, immunocompromise, or chronic liver disease — all within 2 weeks.
reviewerFlag: Guideline from memory, unconfirmed: ACIP age cutoff of 40 years for vaccine-only post-exposure prophylaxis should be verified.

subtopic: Ductus arteriosus pharmacology and duct-dependent congenital heart disease
vignette: A term male infant is born by spontaneous vaginal delivery after an uncomplicated pregnancy. At 30 hours of life he becomes dusky during feeding, and pulse oximetry reads 68% that does not improve with 100% fraction of inspired oxygen. Physical examination shows no murmur and clear lungs. Chest radiograph shows a normal-sized heart. Over the next six hours his oxygen saturation falls further and he becomes lethargic. The care team administers a prostaglandin E1 infusion, and within two hours his saturation rises to 82%.
leadIn: By which mechanism did the prostaglandin E1 infusion improve this infant's oxygenation?

options.a: Increased pulmonary vascular resistance, diverting desaturated blood to the systemic circulation
options.b: Closure of the ductus venosus, increasing hepatic oxygen delivery
options.c: Increased contractility of the right ventricle, raising cardiac output across the pulmonary valve
options.d: Stimulation of surfactant secretion, improving alveolar oxygen diffusion
options.e: Relaxation of ductal smooth muscle, maintaining blood flow from the aorta to the pulmonary artery

explanation: Cyanosis that does not correct with 100% oxygen plus **decreased pulmonary vascular markings** and a single S2 points to an obstructive right-heart lesion such as **pulmonary atresia**, in which pulmonary blood flow depends entirely on the **ductus arteriosus**. As the ductus closes over the first days of life, flow to the lungs falls and the infant desaturates. **Prostaglandin E1** acts on EP receptors on ductal smooth muscle, and the key mechanism is that it **relaxes ductal smooth muscle to keep the ductus patent**, preserving aorta-to-pulmonary-artery flow and improving oxygenation.

distractorExplanations.a: Increasing pulmonary vascular resistance would worsen cyanosis in any lesion by further reducing pulmonary blood flow; this reverses the physiology of duct-dependent lesions.
distractorExplanations.b: The ductus venosus shunts portal blood to the IVC in fetal life and has no role in pulmonary blood flow or systemic oxygenation after birth.
distractorExplanations.c: In pulmonary atresia there is no patent pulmonary valve for the right ventricle to eject across, so increased contractility cannot restore pulmonary flow.
distractorExplanations.d: Surfactant reduces alveolar surface tension, and this infant's lungs are clear with no respiratory distress; his hypoxemia is structural, from inadequate pulmonary blood flow.

teachingPoint: Prostaglandins keep the ductus arteriosus open (PGE1 infusion for duct-dependent cyanotic lesions); NSAIDs close it (indomethacin for PDA). The mechanism both ways is prostaglandin-mediated ductal smooth muscle tone.

subtopic: Thyroid nodule — Bethesda VI, extent of surgery and neck dissection
vignette: A 47-year-old woman is evaluated for a 3.2-cm left thyroid nodule found on palpation during a routine physical. She has no history of head or neck irradiation and no family history of thyroid cancer. TSH is 2.4 mIU/L. Thyroid ultrasound shows a solid, hypoechoic 3.2-cm nodule in the left lobe with microcalcifications and irregular margins; no contralateral thyroid nodules are present. Ultrasound-guided FNA cytology is diagnostic for papillary thyroid carcinoma (Bethesda VI).
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate surgical approach for this patient?

options.a: Total thyroidectomy with prophylactic bilateral central neck dissection
options.b: Left thyroid lobectomy alone
options.c: Diagnostic left thyroid lobectomy with intraoperative frozen section
options.d: Left thyroid lobectomy with ipsilateral prophylactic central neck dissection
options.e: Total thyroidectomy with modified radical neck dissection

explanation: This patient has **Bethesda VI** cytology diagnostic for **papillary thyroid carcinoma**. The tumour is **<4 cm**, confined to one lobe with **no extrathyroidal extension**, no contralateral nodules, and no history of radiation — criteria that make **lobectomy** an adequate surgical extent rather than total thyroidectomy. The ultrasound shows **no suspicious lymphadenopathy**, and current guidelines do not mandate **prophylactic central neck dissection** for low-risk, clinically node-negative papillary thyroid carcinoma. Therefore lobectomy alone is the appropriate operation.

distractorExplanations.a: Total thyroidectomy with prophylactic central neck dissection is indicated for tumours >4 cm, extrathyroidal extension, or clinically apparent nodal disease; none of these are present, and overtreatment risks recurrent laryngeal nerve injury and hypoparathyroidism.
distractorExplanations.c: Frozen section is not routinely needed when cytology is already Bethesda VI; the diagnosis is established and the operation should proceed as a definitive lobectomy.
distractorExplanations.d: Prophylactic central neck dissection may be considered for higher-risk tumours or when nodal metastasis is suspected, but is not routinely indicated for a clinically node-negative low-risk papillary carcinoma <4 cm; adding it increases risk of hypoparathyroidism without proven benefit.
distractorExplanations.e: Modified radical neck dissection is reserved for confirmed lateral neck nodal metastasis (clinical N1b); there is no nodal disease here.

teachingPoint: Papillary thyroid carcinoma <4 cm, intrathyroidal, unilateral, with no nodal metastasis and no radiation history can be treated with lobectomy alone. Prophylactic central neck dissection is not routinely indicated for clinically node-negative low-risk disease.
reviewerFlag: Guideline from memory: ATA 2015 guidelines support lobectomy for papillary thyroid carcinoma 1–4 cm without extrathyroidal extension or nodal metastasis; prophylactic central neck dissection recommendation for low-risk clinically node-negative disease may vary by guideline update — confirm current ATA position.

subtopic: Post-MI ventricular arrhythmia and ICD indication
vignette: A 59-year-old man is recovering in the coronary care unit on hospital day 2 after an anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction, treated with primary angioplasty and stenting of a proximal left anterior descending occlusion. He has been free of chest pain since reperfusion. This morning, telemetry captures a 30-second run of monomorphic ventricular tachycardia at 160/min; his blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg and he is asymptomatic, and the rhythm terminates spontaneously. He is already receiving aspirin, ticagrelor, metoprolol, lisinopril, and atorvastatin. Serum potassium is 4.0 mEq/L and magnesium is 2.0 mg/dL; troponin is falling appropriately.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate management of this patient's arrhythmia?

options.a: Reassessment of ejection fraction at least 40 days after the infarct
options.b: Immediate electrophysiology study with ablation
options.c: Amiodarone loading followed by lifelong oral therapy
options.d: Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement before discharge
options.e: Lidocaine infusion for 48 hours

explanation: Ventricular tachycardia within the first 48 hours after an acute infarct reflects the **electrical instability of the acutely injured myocardium** and does not by itself establish an ICD indication. The decision that matters is what happens once the myocardium has had time to recover: guidelines require **reassessment of ejection fraction at least 40 days post-MI on optimal medical therapy**, because **stunned myocardium** frequently recovers function, and an ICD implanted too early exposes patients to device complications without benefit. If the EF remains ≤35% at that reassessment, primary-prevention ICD implantation is indicated. His hemodynamically tolerated, self-terminating run needs continued beta blockade and electrolyte vigilance, not an acute intervention.

distractorExplanations.b: Electrophysiology study with ablation is reserved for recurrent sustained VT unresponsive to therapy or specific substrates; a single self-terminating run on day 2 does not warrant this.
distractorExplanations.c: Lifelong amiodarone does not improve mortality in this setting and adds pulmonary, thyroid, and hepatic toxicity; beta blockade is the antiarrhythmic backbone after MI.
distractorExplanations.d: ICD implantation within 40 days of an MI is not indicated even with a low ejection fraction, because recovery of stunned myocardium may eliminate the need and early devices carry harm without proven benefit.
distractorExplanations.e: Prophylactic lidocaine was abandoned decades ago because it increased mortality from asystole despite suppressing ventricular ectopy.

teachingPoint: VT within 48 hours of acute MI is treated acutely but does not mandate an ICD. Reassess EF at ≥40 days post-MI on optimal medical therapy; implant an ICD for primary prevention only if EF remains ≤35%.

subtopic: Chagas myocarditis — histologic finding
vignette: A 52-year-old man is evaluated for progressive dyspnea and leg swelling over the past year. Examination shows jugular venous distention, bibasilar crackles, an S3 gallop, and pitting edema of both legs. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 28% and a small apical aneurysm. Endomyocardial biopsy shows a lymphocytic infiltrate in the myocardium, and a peripheral smear and serology are pending.
leadIn: Which of the following histologic findings is most likely to be present on examination of this patient's myocardial tissue?

options.a: Caseating granulomas with central necrosis
options.b: Multinucleated giant cells with eosinophilic necrosis
options.c: Amastigote-filled pseudocysts within cardiac myocytes
options.d: Fibrinous pericardial exudate with frond-like projections
options.e: Intranuclear viral inclusion bodies with myocyte necrosis

explanation: The combination of a **dilated cardiomyopathy with an apical aneurysm**, GI dysmotility (dysphagia and megacolon), and residence in **rural Latin America** identifies chronic **Chagas disease** caused by *Trypanosoma cruzi*. In infected myocardium, the parasite replicates intracellularly, producing **amastigote-filled pseudocysts within cardiac myocytes** surrounded by a lymphocytic infiltrate — the specific finding that distinguishes Chagas myocarditis from other causes of dilated cardiomyopathy.

distractorExplanations.a: Caseating granulomas suggest tuberculosis or fungal infection, neither of which explains the megacolon and apical aneurysm in this epidemiologic setting.
distractorExplanations.b: Multinucleated giant cells with eosinophilic necrosis characterize giant cell myocarditis, a rapidly progressive disease of younger patients without the GI features of this case.
distractorExplanations.d: A fibrinous pericardial exudate would indicate uremic or viral pericarditis and would not cause the dilated cardiomyopathy or megacolon described.
distractorExplanations.e: Viral inclusions with myocyte necrosis would suggest cytomegalovirus or adenovirus myocarditis, which is acute and lacks the chronic GI dysmotility and apical aneurysm.

teachingPoint: Chronic Chagas disease causes dilated cardiomyopathy with apical aneurysm plus megacolon/megaesophagus; cardiac histology shows amastigote-filled pseudocysts within myocytes.

subtopic: Obstructive PFT pattern with bronchodilator reversibility
vignette: A 28-year-old man presents with a two-year history of episodic wheeze and chest tightness. He has never smoked and works as a software developer. On examination he has scattered expiratory wheezes. Spirometry is performed: FEV1 is 62% of predicted, FVC is 88% of predicted, and the FEV1/FVC ratio is 0.68. His chest radiograph is unremarkable.
leadIn: Which set of findings best characterizes this patient's baseline pulmonary physiology?

options.a: Obstructive pattern with increased total lung capacity and reduced DLCO
options.b: Restrictive pattern with reduced total lung capacity and reduced DLCO
options.c: Obstructive pattern with increased total lung capacity and normal DLCO
options.d: Restrictive pattern with reduced total lung capacity and normal DLCO
options.e: Normal spirometry with reduced DLCO and normal total lung capacity

explanation: The low **FEV1/FVC ratio** with a preserved FVC defines an **obstructive pattern**. In asthma, air trapping during exacerbations and chronic hyperinflation raise the **total lung capacity**, while the alveolar-capillary membrane remains intact, so the **DLCO is normal or even increased**. The 17% absolute improvement in FEV1 after albuterol confirms the reversibility that distinguishes asthma from most other obstructive diseases.

distractorExplanations.a: A reduced DLCO with obstruction and hyperinflation suggests emphysema, where alveolar destruction impairs gas transfer; this patient's young age, no smoking history, and reversibility point away from emphysema.
distractorExplanations.b: A restrictive pattern with reduced DLCO characterizes interstitial lung disease, where both lung volumes and gas transfer fall together; his FVC was preserved and the ratio was reduced.
distractorExplanations.d: A restrictive pattern with normal DLCO suggests chest wall disease or neuromuscular weakness, which would not produce wheezing or a post-bronchodilator response.
distractorExplanations.e: His baseline FEV1 was only 62% of predicted with a reduced ratio, so baseline spirometry is clearly abnormal.

teachingPoint: Asthma shows an obstructive pattern (low FEV1/FVC) with hyperinflation (increased TLC) and a normal or increased DLCO, plus reversibility after a bronchodilator.

vignette: A 29-year-old nulligravid woman with endometriosis confirmed by laparoscopic biopsy 2 years ago returns for follow-up. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 3-cm complex ovarian mass with diffuse low-level internal echoes and no significant flow on Doppler, consistent with an endometrioma. Hemoglobin is 12.8 g/dL and beta-hCG is negative.
leadIn: Which of the following is the best next step in management?

options.a: Begin a progestin-only pill and re-evaluate in 6 months
options.b: Begin a combined oral contraceptive with a different progestin component
options.c: Refer for laparoscopic excision of implants and the ovarian cyst
options.d: Refer for total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy
options.e: Begin danazol and add-back estrogen therapy

explanation: This patient has histologically confirmed endometriosis with pain that has persisted despite an adequate trial of **NSAIDs plus continuous combined hormonal contraception**, the accepted first-line medical therapy. distractorExplanations.b: Switching progestin components is reasonable early in management, but she has already had 14 months of continuous combined hormonal therapy without relief.
distractorExplanations.d: Definitive surgery with hysterectomy and oophorectomy is reserved for women who have completed childbearing and have refractory disease; it is inappropriate for a 29-year-old planning pregnancy.

subtopic: Ring-enhancing brain lesion — incomplete consent for stereotactic biopsy
vignette: A 41-year-old man with HIV and a last CD4 count of 45 cells/mm³ presents with two weeks of progressive left arm weakness and a dull right frontal headache. He is not taking antiretroviral therapy. On examination he has a left pronator drift and mild left-sided hyperreflexia. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain shows a single 3-cm ring-enhancing lesion in the right frontal lobe with surrounding oedema and mild midline shift. Toxoplasma IgG is positive. The neurosurgeon recommends stereotactic brain biopsy and says: "A small sample of the lesion will tell us whether this is an infection or a lymphoma, so we can treat you with the right drugs instead of guessing. The main risks are bleeding into the lesion or new weakness in your left arm."
leadIn: Which element of the BRAN framework has not yet been addressed in this discussion?

options.a: The benefits of the procedure
options.b: The consequences of declining all treatment
options.c: The alternatives to the procedure
options.d: The risks of the procedure
options.e: The benefits and risks of the procedure

explanation: The surgeon has explicitly covered three elements: the **benefits** (a tissue diagnosis distinguishing toxoplasmosis from lymphoma, so treatment is aimed at the right disease), the **risks** (haemorrhage into the lesion, new left arm weakness from the biopsy trajectory), and the **alternatives** (empiric toxoplasmosis therapy with repeat MRI in two weeks — the standard non-operative pathway when toxoplasma IgG is positive). What has not been discussed is the **'Nothing' element**: what happens if the patient declines both biopsy and all treatment — namely progressive mass effect, herniation risk and death from an untreated lesion. Until that is covered, the patient cannot weigh doing nothing against the options presented, and consent is incomplete.

distractorExplanations.a: The benefits were stated: tissue diagnosis that distinguishes infection from lymphoma and directs correct therapy.
distractorExplanations.c: The alternatives were stated: empiric toxoplasmosis therapy with repeat imaging rather than operation.
distractorExplanations.d: The risks were stated: bleeding into the lesion and new left arm weakness.
distractorExplanations.e: Both benefits and risks were explicitly discussed; the missing element is what happens if all intervention is declined.

teachingPoint: The 'Nothing' element of BRAN requires telling the patient what will happen if no procedure and no treatment are pursued — for a mass lesion with midline shift, that means progressive mass effect and the risk of herniation and death.

subtopic: Cauda equina syndrome — recognition and imaging
vignette: A 52-year-old woman with a history of chronic low back pain presents to the emergency department with worsening lower back pain radiating to both legs over the past 24 hours. She has not had a bowel movement in two days. On examination, there is reduced strength in ankle dorsiflexion bilaterally. Pinprick sensation is diminished over the posterior thighs and medial buttocks. Knee reflexes are 2+ bilaterally; ankle reflexes are absent.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic study?

options.a: CT of the lumbar spine without contrast
options.b: MRI of the lumbar spine with and without contrast
options.c: MRI of the lumbar spine without contrast
options.d: Plain radiographs of the lumbar spine
options.e: Electromyography and nerve conduction studies

explanation: This patient has **cauda equina syndrome**: bilateral radicular leg pain, **saddle anesthesia**, **urinary retention**, and reduced anal sphincter tone. The cauda equina contains the lumbosacral nerve roots, and compression below the L1–L2 level produces this constellation of findings. **Emergent MRI without contrast** of the lumbar spine is the study of choice to identify the level and cause of compression — most commonly a large central disc herniation — and to guide urgent surgical decompression.

distractorExplanations.a: CT of the lumbar spine can show bony pathology and acute hemorrhage but does not adequately visualize the nerve roots or a herniated disc compressing the cauda equina.
distractorExplanations.b: Contrast is unnecessary when the concern is a herniated disc or bony stenosis; contrast-enhanced MRI is reserved for suspected tumor, infection, or prior lumbar surgery.
distractorExplanations.d: Plain radiographs cannot visualize neural structures or disc tissue and have no role in the diagnosis of cauda equina compression.
distractorExplanations.e: Electrodiagnostic studies are used for chronic radicular or neuropathic evaluation over weeks to months and have no role in an acute myelopathic or cauda equina emergency.

teachingPoint: Cauda equina syndrome presents with bilateral leg pain, saddle anesthesia, urinary retention, and reduced anal sphincter tone. Emergent non-contrast MRI of the lumbar spine is the diagnostic study of choice to confirm compression and guide surgical decompression.

options.b: Digoxin
options.c: Amlodipine
options.d: Isosorbide dinitrate
options.e: Amiodarone

subtopic: Mature cystic teratoma (dermoid cyst) — histologic identification
vignette: A 26-year-old woman undergoes a laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy for a 4-cm cyst that was incidentally found on a pelvic ultrasound. On gross examination, the cystic mass contains a thick yellow material. Microscopic sections show a cyst wall lined by squamous epithelium with underlying sebaceous glands.
leadIn: The presence of tissue from all three germ cell layers in this neoplasm is most consistent with which of the following origins?

options.a: Ovarian surface epithelium
options.b: Primordial germ cell
options.c: Ovarian stromal cell
options.d: Mesothelial cell
options.e: Endodermal sinus cell

explanation: The gross findings of hair, teeth, and sebaceous material are pathognomonic for a **mature cystic teratoma (dermoid cyst)**, the most common ovarian germ cell tumor. These tumors arise from a single **primordial germ cell** and contain differentiated tissue from all three germ layers: ectoderm (squamous epithelium, hair, teeth), mesoderm (muscle, bone), and endoderm (thyroid tissue, gastrointestinal epithelium). The presence of thyroid tissue specifically confirms the inclusion of endodermal derivatives.

distractorExplanations.a: Ovarian surface epithelium gives rise to serous and mucinous cystadenomas, which do not contain tissue from multiple germ layers.
distractorExplanations.c: Ovarian stromal cells give rise to sex cord-stromal tumors such as fibromas and granulosa cell tumors, not teratomas.
distractorExplanations.d: Mesothelial cells are the origin of ovarian surface epithelial tumors, not germ cell tumors.
distractorExplanations.e: Endodermal sinus cells are associated with yolk sac tumors, which produce alpha-fetoprotein and do not contain mature tissue from all three germ layers.

teachingPoint: Mature cystic teratomas are the most common ovarian germ cell tumor, arising from primordial germ cells. They characteristically contain tissue from all three germ layers, with ectodermal elements (hair, teeth, sebaceous glands) being most prominent. A rare complication is struma ovarii, in which thyroid tissue is the predominant component and can cause hyperthyroidism.

subtopic: Knee dislocation — vascular injury and imaging
vignette: A 28-year-old man is brought to the trauma bay after a high-speed motor vehicle collision in which his knee struck the dashboard. He reports severe right knee pain. Blood pressure is 134/82 mmHg, heart rate 96 bpm. The right knee is grossly deformed with posterior displacement of the tibia relative to the femur. Distal pulses are palpable. Sensation is intact throughout the right leg. The knee is splinted and reduced with inline traction, and post-reduction radiographs confirm congruent reduction.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.a: CT angiogram of the right lower extremity
options.b: Admit for serial ABI measurements every 4 hours for 24 hours
options.c: Emergent surgical exploration of the popliteal artery
options.d: Conventional angiography in the interventional radiology suite
options.e: Discharge with knee immobilizer and outpatient follow-up in 1 week

explanation: Posterior knee dislocation from a dashboard mechanism carries a high rate of **popliteal artery injury** because the vessel is tethered behind the tibia and cannot tolerate the posterior displacement force. Although distal pulses are present, the **ABI of 0.82** is abnormal (below the 0.9 threshold), which mandates vascular imaging. **CT angiography** is the current first-line study because it is rapidly available, noninvasive, and highly sensitive for intimal injuries, pseudoaneurysms, and thromboses that may not be apparent on physical examination alone. An initially normal pulse exam does not exclude a popliteal intimal tear, which can progress to delayed thrombosis and limb-threatening ischemia.

distractorExplanations.b: Serial ABI monitoring is appropriate only when the ABI is normal (≥0.9) after reduction; an abnormal ABI mandates immediate imaging.
distractorExplanations.c: Emergent surgical exploration is reserved for signs of limb ischemia — absent pulses, a cold pale foot, or an expanding hematoma — not for an abnormal ABI alone, which first requires imaging to localize the injury.
distractorExplanations.d: Conventional angiography offers excellent imaging but is less readily available, more invasive, and slower to obtain than CT angiography, which is now preferred for initial evaluation.
distractorExplanations.e: Discharge is contraindicated after knee dislocation with an abnormal ABI; occult vascular injury can progress to limb-threatening ischemia.

teachingPoint: Any knee dislocation with ABI < 0.9 mandates CT angiography, even if distal pulses are palpable. Popliteal artery intimal injuries can progress to thrombosis with initially normal examinations.

subtopic: Transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy — distinguishing ATTR from AL and treatment selection
vignette: A 76-year-old man is evaluated for eight months of progressive exertional dyspnea and orthopnea. He describes the sensation of his heart pounding when he lies on his left side. He has a remote six-year history of hypertension that resolved without medication changes. Medications are lisinopril and furosemide; the furosemide was recently increased with little improvement in his edema. On examination, blood pressure is 104/62 mm Hg, pulse is 88/min and irregularly irregular. Jugular venous pressure is 11 cm. Lung bases are dull with fine crackles. There is 3+ pretibial edema. ECG shows low-voltage QRS complexes, a first-degree AV block, and atrial fibrillation. Echocardiography shows concentric biventricular wall thickening with a sparkling-appearing myocardium, a preserved ejection fraction, and grade II diastolic dysfunction. Troponin T is mildly elevated and NT-proBNP is markedly elevated.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic study?

options.a: Cardiac MRI with late gadolinium enhancement
options.b: Endomyocardial biopsy with Congo red staining
options.c: Technetium-99m pyrophosphate scintigraphy
options.d: Serum free light-chain assay in three months
options.e: Coronary CT angiography

explanation: Concentric wall thickening with a **low-voltage ECG** and diastolic dysfunction identifies an **infiltrative cardiomyopathy**, and the long-standing **bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome** points toward amyloid. The negative **serum and urine immunofixation and normal free light-chain ratio** exclude AL amyloidosis, leaving **transthyretin (ATTR) cardiac amyloidosis** as the cause. Because AL has been ruled out serologically, **technetium-99m pyrophosphate scintigraphy** can noninvasively confirm ATTR by demonstrating intense myocardial uptake, sparing this frail patient an endomyocardial biopsy — which is reserved for cases where AL cannot be excluded.

distractorExplanations.b: Biopsy is the gold standard, but once AL is excluded serologically, a positive pyrophosphate scan confirms ATTR without the procedural risk in an elderly patient with heart failure.

distractorExplanations.e: Coronary CT angiography evaluates epicardial coronary disease, which would not explain low voltage, biventricular thickening, and diastolic dysfunction with a preserved ejection fraction.

subtopic: Pediatric renal tumors — Wilms tumor cell of origin
vignette: A 3-year-old girl is brought to her pediatrician because her mother noticed a fullness in her abdomen while bathing her. The child has been eating normally and has had no fevers or weight loss. Examination reveals a firm, smooth, non-tender mass in the left flank that does not cross the midline. Her blood pressure is 138/92 mmHg, and urinalysis shows 10–15 RBC/hpf with no casts. Serum LDH is normal. Abdominal ultrasound shows a large retroperitoneal mass with a pseudocapsule.
leadIn: This tumor most likely arose from which of the following embryologic cells?

options.a: Neural crest sympathoadrenal progenitor
options.b: Metanephric blastema
options.c: Primitive neuroectodermal cell
options.d: Pluripotent embryonal cell of the gonad
options.e: Hepatoblast precursor

explanation: A painless flank mass with **hypertension**, hematuria, and a **claw sign** on ultrasound in a young child is classic for **Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma)**. The hypertension reflects renin secretion by the tumor. Wilms tumor arises from persistent **metanephric blastema** — the primitive metanephric mesenchyme that normally differentiates into mature nephrons — and is associated with loss of **WT1**, as seen in WAGR and Denys-Drash syndromes. Failure of these embryonal renal precursors to mature leaves nests of blastemal cells (nephrogenic rests) that can proliferate into a triphasic tumor containing blastema, stroma, and epithelium.

distractorExplanations.a: The neural crest sympathoadrenal precursor gives rise to neuroblastoma, which typically crosses the midline, secretes catecholamines (elevated VMA/HVA), and causes fever and weight loss — the normal VMA here argues against it.
distractorExplanations.c: Primitive neuroectodermal cells give rise to tumors such as medulloblastoma and Ewing sarcoma, not renal masses.
distractorExplanations.d: Pluripotent embryonal cells of the gonad give rise to germ cell tumors such as yolk sac tumor and teratoma, which arise in the gonads or midline, not in the kidney.
distractorExplanations.e: Hepatoblast precursors give rise to hepatoblastoma, an infantile liver tumor presenting with a right upper quadrant mass and often elevated alpha-fetoprotein.

teachingPoint: Wilms tumor = nephroblastoma from metanephric blastema, associated with WT1 loss (WAGR, Denys-Drash, Beckwith-Wiedemann). Wilms: age ~3, hypertension, hematuria, claw sign. Neuroblastoma: age <2, sympathetic chain, catecholamines, crosses midline.

vignette: A 68-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with two episodes of large-volume maroon-coloured stool followed by hematochezia. Her past medical history is notable for diverticulosis, hypertension, and osteoarthritis. Her blood pressure is 104/62 mmHg and her heart rate is 112/min. She is given 1.5 litres of crystalloid and 1 unit of packed red blood cells, and her blood pressure stabilises at 118/72 mmHg. Her hemoglobin is 7.8 g/dL. Colonoscopy is performed within 6 hours and reveals active arterial spurting from a diverticulum in the sigmoid colon. Epinephrine is injected and two hemoclips are placed, and she remains hemodynamically stable overnight.

options.a: Segmental colectomy via laparotomy
options.b: Technetium-99m tagged red blood cell scintigraphy
options.c: Mesenteric angiography with selective embolization
options.d: Capsule endoscopy
options.e: Octreotide infusion and observation

explanation: This patient has a **diverticular hemorrhage** that was localized by colonoscopy but could not be controlled endoscopically, as evidenced by recurrent bleeding despite epinephrine injection and hemoclips. After failed endoscopic therapy in a patient who has been resuscitated and stabilized, **mesenteric angiography with selective embolization** is the standard next step. Angiography can both localize the bleeding vessel and deliver superselective coil or particle embolization, with a high success rate and lower morbidity than emergent surgery. Surgery is reserved for patients in whom angiographic embolization fails or who are too unstable to tolerate it.

distractorExplanations.a: Segmental colectomy is the salvage therapy for lower GI bleeding when both endoscopic and angiographic control have failed, or when the patient is too unstable for angiography; it carries significant morbidity in an elderly patient.

distractorExplanations.d: Capsule endoscopy is for obscure bleeding in stable patients and provides no therapeutic capability.
distractorExplanations.e: Octreotide is used in variceal bleeding from portal hypertension, not in diverticular arterial hemorrhage, and observation alone is unsafe with ongoing active bleeding.

teachingPoint: The algorithm for diverticular bleeding: resuscitate, then colonoscopy. If endoscopic therapy fails to achieve durable hemostasis, proceed to **mesenteric angiography with selective embolization**. Surgery is the last resort after both endoscopic and angiographic approaches fail.

subtopic: Brachial plexus — upper trunk lesion
vignette: A 24-year-old man is evaluated after a motorcycle collision in which his right shoulder was driven forcefully downward. On examination, the right arm hangs adducted and internally rotated at the side, and the forearm is pronated and extended. He is unable to externally rotate the arm at the shoulder, supinate the forearm, or flex the elbow. Sensation is diminished over the lateral forearm. Reflexes at the biceps and brachioradialis are absent, but the triceps reflex is preserved. Hand intrinsic muscle strength and grip are intact.
leadIn: Which structure was most likely injured?

options.a: Upper trunk of the brachial plexus
options.b: C6 nerve root
options.c: Lateral cord of the brachial plexus
options.d: C5 nerve root
options.e: Posterior cord of the brachial plexus

explanation: The pattern of motor loss — absent shoulder abduction, external rotation, elbow flexion, and forearm supination — reflects injury to the C5 and C6 contributions before they divide into anterior and posterior divisions. **The upper trunk of the brachial plexus** carries exactly these combined fibres, and its injury produces the classic **Erb-Duchenne palsy** ("waiter's tip" position). A single root lesion would not simultaneously abolish both biceps and brachioradialis reflexes while sparing all hand function; a cord lesion would additionally disrupt either median or radial downstream branches.

distractorExplanations.b: A C6 root lesion alone would affect biceps and brachioradialis reflexes but would spare most deltoid and infraspinatus function, which are predominantly C5.
distractorExplanations.c: The lateral cord gives rise to the musculocutaneous and lateral median nerves; a lesion here would weaken elbow flexion and forearm flexion but would spare the posterior cord muscles responsible for shoulder abduction and external rotation.
distractorExplanations.d: A C5 root lesion alone would weaken shoulder abduction and external rotation but would not fully abolish elbow flexion and supination, which depend heavily on C6 contribution to the musculocutaneous nerve.
distractorExplanations.e: The posterior cord gives rise to the axillary and radial nerves; a lesion here would abolish shoulder abduction and extension but would spare elbow flexion and supination carried by the musculocutaneous nerve.

teachingPoint: Erb-Duchenne palsy results from upper trunk (C5–C6) injury, classically from downward traction on the shoulder. The arm adducts and internally rotates (loss of deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus), the elbow extends and the forearm pronates (loss of biceps and supinator), producing the waiter's tip posture. The key anatomical reasoning is that only a trunk-level lesion combines C5 and C6 deficits before anterior/posterior division, while sparing lower trunk hand function.

subtopic: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy — sudden death risk stratification and ICD indication
vignette: A 19-year-old collegiate rower is evaluated after an episode of near-syncope. He was completing an intense interval session when he felt lightheaded and had to stop; he did not lose consciousness. He reports two similar episodes of near-syncope during hard training over the past four months, and occasional exertional chest tightness that resolves with rest. His father is alive and healthy at age 58. On examination, vital signs are normal. Cardiac examination reveals a harsh systolic murmur at the left sternal border that intensifies when the patient performs a Valsalva maneuver and softens with passive leg elevation. The carotid upstrokes are brisk. An ECG shows deep T-wave inversions in the lateral precordial leads and prominent septal Q waves. Echocardiography reports asymmetric septal hypertrophy with a resting left ventricular outflow tract gradient of 25 mm Hg and normal systolic function.
leadIn: In addition to activity restriction, which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient?

options.a: Holter monitoring in three months
options.b: Initiation of oral amiodarone therapy
options.c: Septal myectomy without device therapy
options.d: Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement
options.e: Alcohol septal ablation without device therapy

explanation: Exertional syncope in a young athlete with a **murmur that intensifies with Valsalva** and asymmetric septal hypertrophy establishes **hypertrophic cardiomyopathy** with dynamic outflow tract obstruction. The decision this patient forces is sudden-death prevention, and he carries two major risk factors: **unexplained syncope during exertion** and a **family history of sudden cardiac death** before age 50. Because these risk factors place him at high enough risk for ventricular arrhythmia, the guideline-supported intervention is **implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement** as primary prevention. Medication and septal reduction therapy address the gradient and symptoms, but they do not protect against the arrhythmic event that killed his father.

distractorExplanations.b: Amiodarone suppresses atrial and ventricular ectopy, but it has never been shown to prevent sudden death in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and is not a substitute for device therapy in a high-risk patient.
distractorExplanations.c: Septal myectomy relieves outflow obstruction and symptoms but does not reduce the risk of ventricular fibrillation, which is the threat signaled by his syncope and family history.
distractorExplanations.e: Alcohol septal ablation reduces the gradient but creates scar that can itself be arrhythmogenic, and like myectomy it does not address his sudden-death risk.

teachingPoint: In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, exertional syncope plus a family history of sudden cardiac death are major sudden-death risk factors; the intervention that addresses that risk is an ICD, not gradient-reducing therapy.

subtopic: Thalassemia trait versus iron deficiency
vignette: A 26-year-old woman is evaluated during a pre-employment health examination. She feels well and reports no fatigue, no heavy menstrual bleeding, and a diet that includes red meat several times weekly. She takes no medications. Her physical examination is unremarkable. A complete blood count ordered as part of the examination shows hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 66 fL, red blood cell count 6.1 million/μL, and normal white blood cell and platelet counts. The peripheral smear shows microcytic cells with minimal variation in shape and no target cells.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

options.a: Order hemoglobin electrophoresis
options.b: Measure soluble transferrin receptor concentration
options.c: Perform upper and lower gastrointestinal endoscopy
options.d: Begin a 3-month trial of oral iron supplementation
options.e: Repeat the complete blood count in 6 months

explanation: This patient's iron studies are normal, so her **microcytosis is not iron deficiency**. The key clue is **disproportionate microcytosis**: a mean corpuscular volume of 66 fL with a hemoglobin of 11.9 g/dL is far more microcytosis than the degree of anemia explains, and the **elevated red blood cell count** is characteristic of thalassemia trait, in which the marrow compensates for small cells by producing more of them. Her Mediterranean ancestry and the **Mentzer index** (MCV divided by RBC count, less than 13) both point to **thalassemia trait**. **Hemoglobin electrophoresis** is the confirmatory study, showing an elevated hemoglobin A2 in beta-thalassemia trait. No iron should be given, since her stores are already normal.

distractorExplanations.b: Soluble transferrin receptor is elevated in iron deficiency, which her normal iron studies already exclude.
distractorExplanations.c: Endoscopic evaluation is indicated for iron deficiency anemia in men and postmenopausal women; this premenopausal woman has no iron deficiency at all.
distractorExplanations.d: Iron therapy would do nothing here because her ferritin and iron studies are normal, and it risks iron overload in a patient who does not need it.
distractorExplanations.e: Deferring evaluation leaves a heritable hemoglobinopathy, relevant to future pregnancy counseling, undiagnosed.

teachingPoint: Microcytosis out of proportion to anemia, an elevated RBC count, normal iron studies, and a Mentzer index under 13 point to thalassemia trait, confirmed by hemoglobin electrophoresis with elevated hemoglobin A2.

subtopic: Acute Coronary Syndrome — Prinzmetal angina diagnosis
vignette: A 36-year-old woman presents with a 2-week history of chest pain occurring each morning between 5 and 6 a.m., waking her from sleep. Each episode lasts 8 minutes and resolves spontaneously. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 18 years. She takes no medications and has no chronic medical conditions. Vital signs are unremarkable. High-sensitivity troponin T is 9 ng/L (reference <14).
leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?

options.a: Epicardial coronary artery spasm at the site of a non-occlusive plaque
options.b: Atherosclerotic plaque rupture with transient thrombotic occlusion
options.c: Embolization of a coronary thrombus originating in the left atrial appendage
options.d: Fixed high-grade stenosis of the right coronary artery from atherosclerosis
options.e: Microvascular dysfunction with normal epicardial coronary arteries

explanation: This is **Prinzmetal (variant) angina**, caused by **epicardial coronary artery vasospasm**, typically at the site of a non-occlusive atherosclerotic plaque. The classic pattern is rest angina in a younger patient, often occurring in the early morning hours, with **transient ST-segment elevation** that resolves with nitrates and a troponin below the 99th percentile, indicating ischemia without infarction. Smoking is the strongest risk factor. The absence of exertional symptoms argues against a fixed obstructive stenosis, which characteristically produces symptoms with activity rather than at rest.

distractorExplanations.b: Plaque rupture with thrombotic occlusion produces a STEMI with a persistently elevated troponin, not transient ST elevation that resolves within minutes with a normal troponin.
distractorExplanations.c: Coronary embolism from a left atrial appendage thrombus requires atrial fibrillation or another source of stasis, none of which is present.
distractorExplanations.d: A fixed high-grade right coronary artery stenosis would produce exertional angina rather than exclusively rest angina, and the ST elevation would not resolve within minutes without infarction.
distractorExplanations.e: Microvascular dysfunction produces angina with normal epicardial arteries and no ECG changes; the transient ST elevation localizes the process to an epicardial vessel.

teachingPoint: Prinzmetal (variant) angina = rest angina, classically in the early morning, with transient ST-segment elevation that resolves with nitrates and a normal troponin — caused by epicardial coronary vasospasm, usually at the site of a non-occlusive plaque. Smoking is the leading risk factor.

subtopic: Chronic HFrEF — drug selection in a potassium-constrained patient
vignette: A 72-year-old woman with a history of nonischemic cardiomyopathy is evaluated in the cardiology clinic for persistent exertional dyspnea. Her left ventricular ejection fraction was 28% on echocardiography two months ago. She currently takes carvedilol 25 mg twice daily and lisinopril 20 mg daily, both at maximally tolerated doses. She reports dyspnea after walking one block on level ground and sleeps with two pillows. The blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg, heart rate 64/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. The jugular venous pressure is 8 cm. There is no lower extremity edema. Laboratory studies show a serum sodium of 136 mEq/L. An echocardiogram today shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 30% with no pericardial effusion.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate medication to add to this patient's regimen at this time?

options.a: Spironolactone 25 mg orally daily
options.b: Furosemide 40 mg orally daily
options.c: Digoxin 0.125 mg orally daily
options.d: Hydralazine 25 mg and isosorbide dinitrate 20 mg orally three times daily
options.e: Dapagliflozin 10 mg orally daily

explanation: This patient has **HFrEF** with persistent symptoms despite a beta-blocker and an ACE inhibitor at maximally tolerated doses, so guideline-directed medical therapy must be intensified. The **potassium of 5.3 mEq/L and creatinine of 2.1 mg/dL** contraindicate adding a **mineralocorticoid antagonist**, which requires potassium below 5.0 and an eGFR above 30 to mitigate life-threatening hyperkalemia. **SGLT2 inhibitors** reduce heart failure hospitalization and cardiovascular mortality in HFrEF regardless of diabetic status, and their benefit is independent of the potassium and renal thresholds that limit MRA initiation. Dapagliflozin is therefore the safest and most effective agent to add under these constraints.

distractorExplanations.a: Spironolactone is a cornerstone of HFrEF therapy but is contraindicated when potassium exceeds 5.0 mEq/L or eGFR is below 30, as this patient's values demonstrate; initiating it risks life-threatening hyperkalemia.
distractorExplanations.b: Furosemide is appropriate for volume overload, but this patient has no edema and a JVP of 8 cm; adding a loop diuretic does not address the need to intensify disease-modifying neurohormonal therapy.
distractorExplanations.c: Digoxin reduces heart failure hospitalizations but has no mortality benefit and is reserved for symptom control when first-line therapies are exhausted or rate control in atrial fibrillation is inadequate; it is not the next agent to add when an SGLT2 inhibitor is available.
distractorExplanations.d: The hydralazine-nitrate combination has a mortality benefit in HFrEF, but it is typically reserved for patients who are intolerant to or cannot receive ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy, particularly self-identified African American patients with persistent symptoms; this patient is tolerating lisinopril well.

teachingPoint: When intensifying GDMT in HFrEF, the patient's potassium and renal function determine the sequence. An SGLT2 inhibitor can be added across a broad range of eGFR and does not require potassium to be below a specific threshold, making it the preferred agent when MRA initiation is constrained by hyperkalemia or advanced CKD.

subtopic: Hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer — surveillance strategy
vignette: A 28-year-old woman is seen in clinic to establish care after moving to a new city. She feels well and has no gastrointestinal symptoms. Her mother was diagnosed with colorectal cancer at age 42 and died of the disease at age 49. The patient's father is healthy at age 65, and she has one healthy sibling. She takes a combined oral contraceptive pill and no other medications. Physical examination is unremarkable. A complete blood count and liver function tests are normal. She has never undergone colonoscopy. She inquires about what screening she should pursue.
leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step in this patient's management?

options.a: Referral for germline mismatch repair gene testing
options.b: Annual fecal immunochemical test starting now
options.c: Colonoscopy every 1 to 2 years starting at age 25
options.d: Colonoscopy every 5 years starting at age 40
options.e: Annual screening with capsule endoscopy starting at age 30

explanation: This patient's family history meets the **Amsterdam II criteria** for suspected **Lynch syndrome**: three relatives with Lynch-associated cancers (colorectal cancer in her mother and uncle, endometrial cancer in her grandmother) across two generations, one being a first-degree relative of the other two, and at least one diagnosis before age 50. The appropriate next step is **germline genetic testing for mismatch repair gene mutations**. Identifying the specific mutation (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, or EPCAM) determines whether the patient carries the family mutation and guides the intensity and timing of cancer surveillance, including colonoscopy every one to two years beginning at age 25 or ten years before the youngest affected relative's diagnosis.

distractorExplanations.b: Fecal immunochemical testing is a standard average-risk screening tool and is insufficient for a patient with a family history suggestive of Lynch syndrome, where colonoscopic surveillance is required once the diagnosis is confirmed.
distractorExplanations.c: While colonoscopy every 1–2 years starting at age 25 is the recommended surveillance for confirmed Lynch syndrome carriers, this patient has not yet undergone genetic testing to confirm she carries the mutation.
distractorExplanations.d: A 5-year colonoscopy interval starting at age 40 is appropriate for patients with a single first-degree relative diagnosed after age 60, not for those with a family history meeting Amsterdam II criteria.
distractorExplanations.e: Capsule endoscopy is not a recommended screening modality for colorectal cancer surveillance in Lynch syndrome or any other high-risk setting.

teachingPoint: Patients whose family history meets Amsterdam II criteria should undergo germline genetic testing for mismatch repair gene mutations before initiating intensified cancer surveillance. The specific mutation identified determines the surveillance strategy, which typically includes colonoscopy every 1–2 years beginning at age 25 or ten years before the earliest diagnosed relative.

subtopic: Fabry disease — lysosomal Gb3 deposition causing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
vignette: A 26-year-old man is evaluated for progressive shortness of breath on exertion over the past year, occasionally accompanied by lightheadedness and one episode of exertional syncope. He has no history of recurrent pain episodes, and he reports normal sweating. Examination shows a harsh systolic murmur at the left sternal border that increases with the Valsalva maneuver. Urinalysis is unremarkable. Transthoracic echocardiography shows asymmetric thickening of the interventricular septum with systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve and dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. Serum leukocyte alpha-galactosidase A activity is normal. His maternal uncle died suddenly at age 42 while playing basketball.
leadIn: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of this patient's cardiomyopathy?

options.a: Deposition of insoluble fibrillar proteins in the extracellular matrix with amyloid-positive Congo red staining
options.b: Iron deposition within myocardial cells with reactive oxidative injury and fibrosis
options.c: Accumulation of globotriaosylceramide within lysosomes of myocardial cells
options.d: Autoimmune myocyte injury following a viral infection with lymphocytic infiltration
options.e: Sarcomere protein mutation causing myocyte disarray with asymmetric septal hypertrophy

explanation: This patient has **Fabry disease**, an **X-linked lysosomal storage disorder** caused by deficiency of **alpha-galactosidase A**. Because the deficient enzyme normally cleaves the terminal galactose from **globotriaosylceramide (Gb3)**, the substrate accumulates within lysosomes of endothelial, renal, and cardiac cells. The cardiac consequence is **Gb3 accumulation within lysosomes of myocardial cells**, which produces concentric hypertrophy with a characteristic speckled, ground-glass appearance on echocardiography and eventual diastolic dysfunction. The other features anchor the diagnosis: heat-triggered neuropathic pain, hypohidrosis, **angiokeratomas**, and proteinuria from renal deposition.

distractorExplanations.a: Amyloid deposition, as in AL or transthyretin amyloidosis, produces a restrictive cardiomyopathy with Congo red–positive extracellular fibrils, not lysosomal storage; the reduced alpha-galactosidase A activity excludes it.
distractorExplanations.b: Iron deposition from hereditary hemochromatosis can cause a dilated or restrictive cardiomyopathy, but it does not cause neuropathic pain, angiokeratomas, or reduced alpha-galactosidase A activity.
distractorExplanations.d: Viral myocarditis causes a dilated cardiomyopathy with lymphocytic infiltration and elevated troponin, not concentric hypertrophy with a storage-disorder phenotype.
distractorExplanations.e: A sarcomere protein mutation causes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with asymmetric septal hypertrophy and myocyte disarray, which does not fit the lysosomal enzyme deficiency or the systemic findings here.

teachingPoint: Fabry disease — X-linked alpha-galactosidase A deficiency — causes globotriaosylceramide to accumulate in myocardial lysosomes, producing concentric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with a speckled, ground-glass echocardiographic appearance.
reviewerFlag: The speckled ground-glass echocardiographic appearance of Fabry cardiomyopathy is from memory, unconfirmed.

subtopic: Acute upper GI bleeding — resuscitation and endoscopy timing
vignette: A 68-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after vomiting bright red blood and coffee-ground material at home, followed by a large black stool. He has a history of osteoarthritis, for which he takes ibuprofen 600 mg twice daily and low-dose aspirin 81 mg daily. He also takes metoprolol for hypertension. On arrival, he appears comfortable. Vital signs are blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, heart rate 88 bpm, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He is alert and answers questions appropriately. Abdominal examination reveals epigastric tenderness without guarding; rectal examination shows maroon-coloured stool. Two large-bore peripheral IV catheters are placed, and he has received 1 L of isotonic crystalloid with stable vital signs. Stat laboratory results show hemoglobin of 9.8 g/dL. The nurse asks what to do next.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate next step in this patient's management?

options.a: Administer IV omeprazole 80 mg bolus followed by 8 mg/hour infusion
options.b: Perform emergent upper endoscopy within 12 hours
options.c: Begin rapid isotonic crystalloid infusion and prepare for blood transfusion
options.d: Administer IV erythromycin 250 mg to improve endoscopic visualisation
options.e: Administer IV octreotide 50 mcg bolus followed by 50 mcg/hour infusion

explanation: This patient presents with **acute upper GI bleeding** (haematemesis and melena) in the setting of chronic NSAID and aspirin use, and he is in **haemorrhagic shock** (hypotension, tachycardia, altered mental status). The immediate priority in any unstable GI bleed is **volume resuscitation** with rapid isotonic crystalloid infusion and preparation for blood transfusion to restore tissue perfusion before any diagnostic or therapeutic intervention. Endoscopy within 12 hours, IV PPI infusion, and prokinetic agents all have roles in upper GI bleeding management, but they must follow initial resuscitation.

distractorExplanations.a: IV PPI infusion is part of upper GI bleeding management but is initiated after or alongside resuscitation, not before haemodynamic stability is achieved.
distractorExplanations.b: Emergent endoscopy within 12 hours is indicated for diagnosis and haemostasis but must follow initial stabilisation; performing endoscopy in an unstable, under-resuscitated patient increases procedural risk.
distractorExplanations.d: IV erythromycin improves gastric visualisation during endoscopy but is an adjunct given 30–90 minutes before the procedure, not the first intervention in a patient in haemorrhagic shock.
distractorExplanations.e: IV octreotide reduces splanchnic blood flow and is used when variceal bleeding is suspected, but this patient's NSAID use and epigastric tendibility favour a non-variceal source; regardless, resuscitation takes priority over any pharmacotherapy.

teachingPoint: In any patient presenting with acute GI bleeding and signs of **haemorrhagic shock** (hypotension, tachycardia, altered mental status), the first and most critical step is **volume resuscitation** with isotonic crystalloid and preparation for transfusion. All subsequent interventions — IV PPI infusion, octreotide for suspected variceal bleeding, erythromycin for endoscopic visualisation, and **urgent endoscopy within 12 hours** — must follow or accompany initial haemodynamic stabilisation, never precede it.

subtopic: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy — sudden death prevention
vignette: A 24-year-old man is evaluated in cardiology clinic after an episode of syncope during a competitive basketball game. He lost consciousness for roughly 20 seconds while sprinting and awoke with confusion that cleared within a minute. He has had progressive exertional dyspnea and orthopnea for the past year despite maximal tolerated doses of beta blockers, with two hospitalizations for acute decompensated heart failure in the past 6 months; he has no chest pain. His father died suddenly at age 34 while swimming; an autopsy was never performed. He takes no medications and does not smoke. Blood pressure is 98/64 mmHg and pulse is 92/min. Cardiac examination reveals a harsh systolic ejection murmur at the left sternal border that increases with standing and decreases with squatting, bibasilar crackles, and an S3 gallop; jugular venous pressure is 12 cm of water. ECG shows deep T-wave inversions in the lateral precordial leads and low voltage. Echocardiography demonstrates asymmetric septal hypertrophy with a maximal wall thickness of 20 mm, systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve, a resting left ventricular outflow tract gradient of 60 mmHg, severe biatrial enlargement, and a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 22% with global hypokinesis. He is started on a beta blocker and counseled to avoid competitive athletics.
leadIn: In addition to the beta blocker and activity restriction, which of the following is the most appropriate next step to reduce this patient's risk of death?

options.a: Subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator implantation
options.b: Cardiac transplantation evaluation
options.c: Permanent pacemaker implantation for syncope prevention
options.d: Septal myectomy to relieve the outflow tract gradient
options.e: Amiodarone therapy for ventricular arrhythmia suppression

explanation: This patient has obstructive **hypertrophic cardiomyopathy**, and his syncope on exertion plus a **family history of sudden cardiac death** place him at high risk for **sudden cardiac death** from ventricular arrhythmia. Beta blockers and activity restriction address symptoms and exposure, but they do not protect against an arrhythmic arrest; the defibrillator does. Septal reduction is reserved for patients with refractory symptoms despite maximally tolerated medical therapy, and this patient has only New York Heart Association class II symptoms at first presentation.

distractorExplanations.c: Pacing does not prevent sudden arrhythmic death; it is indicated for conduction disease or bradyarrhythmias, neither of which this patient has.
distractorExplanations.d: Septal myectomy or alcohol ablation improves symptoms and gradient in patients refractory to medical therapy, but gradient reduction has not been established to reduce sudden death risk the way defibrillator implantation has.
distractorExplanations.e: Amiodarone can reduce arrhythmia burden but has not been shown to reduce sudden death risk in HCM and carries substantial long-term toxicity; it does not substitute for defibrillator protection.

subtopic: Nephrotic syndrome — infection risk and prevention
vignette: A 7-year-old girl is seen for routine follow-up of minimal change disease diagnosed 14 months ago. options.c: Abdominal ultrasound every 6 months
options.d: Annual influenza vaccination only
options.e: Monthly intravenous immunoglobulin infusions

subtopic: Cardiac glycosides — mechanism of positive inotropy and AV nodal effects
vignette: A 68-year-old woman with chronic atrial fibrillation and reduced left ventricular systolic function is evaluated for acute decompensated heart failure with dyspnea at rest and cool, poorly perfused extremities. She is started on a continuous intravenous agent that increases myocardial contractility while producing vasodilation. Her ECG four weeks later shows a regularized ventricular rhythm at 58/min with a normal QRS duration.
leadIn: What cellular mechanism is directly responsible for the increased contractility produced by this medication?

options.a: Beta-1 adrenergic receptor activation raising intracellular cAMP
options.b: Reduced Na/Ca exchanger activity raising cytosolic calcium
options.c: Phosphodiesterase-3 inhibition raising intracellular cAMP
options.d: L-type calcium channel phosphorylation increasing calcium influx
options.e: Sarcoplasmic reticulum ryanodine receptor sensitization to calcium

explanation: **Digoxin** inhibits the **Na/K ATPase**, raising intracellular sodium. The resulting reduction in the transmembrane sodium gradient **impairs the Na/Ca exchanger**, so less calcium is extruded from the myocyte and cytosolic calcium accumulates. More calcium available to the contractile apparatus produces the positive inotropic effect, while AV nodal conduction velocity falls because Na/K ATPase suppression also decreases repolarizing reserve in nodal tissue.

distractorExplanations.a: Sympathomimetics raise cAMP via beta-1 stimulation to increase contractility, but they accelerate AV nodal conduction rather than slow it.
distractorExplanations.c: Phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitors like milrinone raise cAMP to increase inotropy, but they do not slow AV nodal conduction and are not used for rate control.
distractorExplanations.d: L-type channel phosphorylation is downstream of beta-adrenergic signaling, not a direct mechanism of Na/K ATPase inhibition.
distractorExplanations.e: Ryanodine receptor sensitization is not a recognized mechanism of digoxin; digoxin acts upstream at the Na/K ATPase to increase SR calcium loading indirectly.

teachingPoint: Digoxin's positive inotropy flows from Na/K ATPase inhibition → reduced Na/Ca exchange → increased intracellular Ca. Its rate-slowing effect in atrial fibrillation comes from enhanced vagal tone and direct AV nodal depression.

vignette: A 56-year-old woman admitted to the intensive care unit develops fever and new leukocytosis on hospital day 9. The organism shows resistance to multiple antibiotics on testing.

options.b: Exotoxin A-mediated tissue necrosis at the catheter insertion site
options.c: IgA protease-mediated colonization of mucosal surfaces
options.d: Intracellular survival within endothelial cells after bloodstream invasion
options.e: Secretion of a polysaccharide glycocalyx forming biofilm on the catheter surface

explanation: Catalase-positive, coagulase-negative gram-positive cocci in clusters from blood cultures in a patient with an indwelling central line identify **Staphylococcus epidermidis**, a classic cause of **coagulase-negative staphylococcal bacteremia** in healthcare settings. Its defining virulence factor is the ability to adhere to inert surfaces and secrete a **polysaccharide glycocalyx (slime) that forms a biofilm on the catheter surface**. The biofilm shields the organism from host phagocytes and antibiotics, which explains both the absence of local site findings and the **multidrug resistance** on susceptibility testing.

distractorExplanations.d: Endothelial intracellular survival is not a staphylococcal epidermidis mechanism; the organism persists extracellularly within biofilm on the device.

teachingPoint: Staphylococcus epidermidis causes healthcare-associated device infections by producing a polysaccharide glycocalyx biofilm on catheter surfaces, which shields it from host defenses and contributes to multidrug resistance.

subtopic: Endometriosis management after failure of first-line medical therapy

subtopic: Breaking bad news (SPIKES)
vignette: A 57-year-old woman is recovering on the ward after a seizure. Imaging obtained overnight shows a large left frontal mass with surrounding edema, and histology from a prior biopsy at another hospital is consistent with a high-grade glioma. On morning rounds, the patient is somnolent and disoriented to time and place, and her husband, who is her designated healthcare proxy, is at the bedside. Before the resident says anything further, the attending takes him aside to review how the conversation should be conducted.
leadIn: Which of the following should the resident do first when he returns to the patient's room?

options.a: State the diagnosis plainly and ask her to sign a consent form for further treatment
options.b: Tell her the results are concerning but reassure her that everything will be fine
options.c: Ask her what she understands so far about why she was transferred to the hospital
options.d: Share the imaging report in full detail and explain each finding sequentially
options.e: Direct the discussion to her husband so the patient is not overwhelmed by the news

explanation: Delivering serious news follows the **SPIKES** framework — setting, perception, invitation, knowledge, emotions, strategy. Before any information is shared, the physician must **assess the patient's perception** of her situation by asking what she already knows or believes. This reveals how much she was told before transfer, frames how much detail to give, and prevents the physician from talking past the patient. Skipping straight to disclosure risks overwhelming her with information she cannot contextualize, and it forfeits the chance to correct misconceptions.

distractorExplanations.b: False reassurance is dishonest and undermines trust; the physician cannot promise a good outcome for a high-grade glioma.
distractorExplanations.d: Reciting the full report without first gauging her understanding and her invitation for detail gives uncontextualized information and is likely to overwhelm her.
distractorExplanations.e: Excluding a capable patient from her own diagnostic discussion is paternalistic; family involvement is encouraged, but the patient remains the primary participant.

teachingPoint: Before delivering bad news, always assess the patient's perception of the situation — SPIKES: Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Emotions, Strategy.

subtopic: Pediatric renal tumors — Wilms tumor cell of origin
vignette: A 3-year-old girl is brought to her pediatrician because her mother noticed a fullness in her abdomen while bathing her. The child has been eating normally and has had no fevers or weight loss. Examination reveals a firm, smooth, non-tender mass in the left upper quadrant that crosses the midline. Her blood pressure is 138/92 mmHg, and urinalysis shows 10–15 RBC/hpf with no casts. Serum LDH is normal, but vanillylmandelic acid is markedly elevated. Abdominal ultrasound shows a large suprarenal mass with areas of calcification; the kidney is compressed but not invaded, and no claw sign is noted.
leadIn: This tumor most likely arose from which of the following embryologic cells?

options.a: Neural crest sympathoadrenal progenitor
options.b: Metanephric blastema
options.c: Primitive neuroectodermal cell
options.d: Pluripotent embryonal cell of the gonad
options.e: Hepatoblast precursor

explanation: A painless flank mass with **hypertension**, hematuria, and a **claw sign** on ultrasound in a young child is classic for **Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma)**. The hypertension reflects renin secretion by the tumor. Wilms tumor arises from persistent **metanephric blastema** — the primitive metanephric mesenchyme that normally differentiates into mature nephrons — and is associated with loss of **WT1**, as seen in WAGR and Denys-Drash syndromes. Failure of these embryonal renal precursors to mature leaves nests of blastemal cells (nephrogenic rests) that can proliferate into a triphasic tumor containing blastema, stroma, and epithelium.

distractorExplanations.a: The neural crest sympathoadrenal precursor gives rise to neuroblastoma, which typically crosses the midline, secretes catecholamines (elevated VMA/HVA), and causes fever and weight loss — the normal VMA here argues against it.
distractorExplanations.c: Primitive neuroectodermal cells give rise to tumors such as medulloblastoma and Ewing sarcoma, not renal masses.
distractorExplanations.d: Pluripotent embryonal cells of the gonad give rise to germ cell tumors such as yolk sac tumor and teratoma, which arise in the gonads or midline, not in the kidney.
distractorExplanations.e: Hepatoblast precursors give rise to hepatoblastoma, an infantile liver tumor presenting with a right upper quadrant mass and often elevated alpha-fetoprotein.

teachingPoint: Wilms tumor = nephroblastoma from metanephric blastema, associated with WT1 loss (WAGR, Denys-Drash, Beckwith-Wiedemann). Wilms: age ~3, hypertension, hematuria, claw sign. Neuroblastoma: age <2, sympathetic chain, catecholamines, crosses midline.

subtopic: Aortic Stenosis — Referred for Valve Replacement
vignette: A 76-year-old man is evaluated for routine follow-up. He denies chest pain, shortness of breath, or syncope, and he remains fully active, walking 2 miles daily without limitation. Past history includes hypertension treated with amlodipine. He has smoked half a pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years. On examination, BP is 145/85 mm Hg and pulse is 78/min and regular. Cardiac auscultation reveals a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to both carotid arteries, with a soft second heart sound. Carotid pulses are delayed in onset and low in amplitude. An echocardiogram shows a calcified, immobile aortic valve with a peak velocity of 4.5 m/s, a mean gradient of 45 mm Hg, and a valve area of 0.7 cm2. Left ventricular systolic function is normal.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.a: Increase the amlodipine dose and reassess symptoms in 3 months
options.b: Refer for dobutamine stress echocardiography
options.c: Repeat echocardiography in 6 to 12 months
options.d: Refer for percutaneous balloon aortic valvuloplasty
options.e: Refer for aortic valve replacement

explanation: This patient has **severe symptomatic aortic stenosis**: a valve area <1 cm2 with a mean gradient >40 mm Hg, plus the classic triad of **exertional angina, dyspnea, and syncope**. Once symptoms develop, the mean survival without valve replacement falls to 2-3 years and sudden death risk rises sharply, so **aortic valve replacement is the only effective treatment** and should be offered promptly regardless of age. Because his left ventricular function is preserved and he has no symptoms at rest, he is a straightforward surgical candidate.

distractorExplanations.b: Stress testing is contraindicated in symptomatic severe aortic stenosis and adds nothing once severity is already established by resting echocardiography.
distractorExplanations.c: Surveillance echocardiography is appropriate only for asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis; symptoms change the decision from watching to replacing.
distractorExplanations.d: Balloon valvuloplasty provides only short-term gradient relief in calcified adult valves and is reserved as a bridge in patients too unstable for definitive valve replacement.

teachingPoint: Symptoms in severe aortic stenosis — angina, dyspnea, or syncope — are the trigger for valve replacement; watchful waiting is for asymptomatic disease only.

subtopic: Cauda equina syndrome — recognition and imaging
vignette: A 52-year-old woman with a history of chronic low back pain presents to the emergency department with worsening lower back pain radiating to both legs over the past 24 hours. She also reports difficulty urinating for the past several hours. She has not had a bowel movement in two days. She has a permanent pacemaker implanted for complete heart block. On examination, there is reduced strength in ankle dorsiflexion bilaterally. Pinprick sensation is diminished over the posterior thighs, perineum, and medial buttocks. A rectal exam reveals reduced anal sphincter tone. Knee reflexes are 2+ bilaterally; ankle reflexes are absent.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic study?

options.a: CT of the lumbar spine without contrast
options.b: MRI of the lumbar spine with and without contrast
options.c: MRI of the lumbar spine without contrast
options.d: Plain radiographs of the lumbar spine
options.e: Electromyography and nerve conduction studies

explanation: This patient has **cauda equina syndrome**: bilateral radicular leg pain, **saddle anesthesia**, **urinary retention**, and reduced anal sphincter tone. The cauda equina contains the lumbosacral nerve roots, and compression below the L1–L2 level produces this constellation of findings. **Emergent MRI without contrast** of the lumbar spine is the study of choice to identify the level and cause of compression — most commonly a large central disc herniation — and to guide urgent surgical decompression.

distractorExplanations.a: CT of the lumbar spine can show bony pathology and acute hemorrhage but does not adequately visualize the nerve roots or a herniated disc compressing the cauda equina.
distractorExplanations.b: Contrast is unnecessary when the concern is a herniated disc or bony stenosis; contrast-enhanced MRI is reserved for suspected tumor, infection, or prior lumbar surgery.
distractorExplanations.d: Plain radiographs cannot visualize neural structures or disc tissue and have no role in the diagnosis of cauda equina compression.
distractorExplanations.e: Electrodiagnostic studies are used for chronic radicular or neuropathic evaluation over weeks to months and have no role in an acute myelopathic or cauda equina emergency.

teachingPoint: Cauda equina syndrome presents with bilateral leg pain, saddle anesthesia, urinary retention, and reduced anal sphincter tone. Emergent non-contrast MRI of the lumbar spine is the diagnostic study of choice to confirm compression and guide surgical decompression.

subtopic: Potassium shifts in DKA
vignette: A 24-year-old man with type 1 diabetes presents with fatigue and weakness. He accidentally took a double dose of his rapid-acting insulin two hours ago and has since had tremor and diaphoresis. His blood glucose is 42 mg/dL, arterial pH is 7.48, and serum potassium is 2.9 mEq/L. The total body potassium stores in this patient are significantly depleted.
leadIn: Which of the following mechanisms most directly explains the elevation of his serum potassium despite total body potassium depletion?

options.a: Activation of the Na+/K+-ATPase in skeletal muscle
options.b: Increased urinary potassium excretion from aldosterone activation
options.c: Inhibition of the Na+/K+-ATPase in skeletal muscle
options.d: Massive intravascular hemolysis releasing intracellular potassium
options.e: Suppression of the Na+/K+-ATPase in the proximal renal tubule

explanation: Insulin normally stimulates the **Na+/K+-ATPase** pump on cell membranes, driving potassium from the extracellular fluid into cells. In DKA, **absolute insulin deficiency** removes this stimulus, causing potassium to shift out of cells into the serum. Concurrent **acidosis** further promotes extracellular potassium shift via intracellular H+ buffering. This produces hyperkalemia even though total body potassium is depleted from osmotic diuresis.

distractorExplanations.a: Activation of the Na+/K+-ATPase would drive potassium intracellularly, producing hypokalemia rather than hyperkalemia.
distractorExplanations.b: Aldosterone does promote urinary potassium loss, but this mechanism explains the total body depletion, not the elevated serum concentration.
distractorExplanations.d: Hemolysis can elevate serum potassium, but there is no clinical evidence of hemolysis in this presentation.
distractorExplanations.e: The Na+/K+-ATPase in the proximal tubule is not the primary determinant of the acute transcellular potassium shift seen in DKA; the major shift occurs in skeletal muscle and liver.

teachingPoint: Hyperkalemia in DKA is a distributional phenomenon caused by insulin deficiency and acidosis driving potassium extracellularly; it masks profound total body potassium depletion.
